seo.title: Buy vs Rent Calculator: Break-Even Year & Net Worth Comparison
seo.description: Free buy vs rent calculator. Compare mortgage, tax, upkeep and opportunity cost against rent to see your break-even year and net worth after 1 to 40 years.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Compare the true long-term cost of owning a home against renting and investing the difference.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Deciding whether to buy a home or keep renting is one of the biggest financial choices most people make. The monthly mortgage payment is only part of the picture. Owners also pay property tax, insurance, maintenance and, when they sell, agent fees and closing costs. Renters avoid those costs, and if they invest the money they would have spent on a down payment and on the gap between owning and renting, that money can grow.

This calculator models both paths month by month. It tracks the owner's home equity after selling costs and the renter's investment portfolio, then shows which side has more net worth after the number of years you plan to stay. It also reports the break-even year, the first year in which buying overtakes renting, or says clearly when it is not reached in your time frame.

The result depends heavily on how long you stay. Upfront costs such as closing fees and selling fees are large compared with a few years of equity growth, so short stays usually favor renting, while long stays give ownership time to build equity. Rent growth, home appreciation and the return on invested savings matter too, which is why the calculator lets you change every one of them.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the home price, down payment, mortgage rate and loan term.
Add ownership costs: property tax, insurance, maintenance, buying closing costs and selling costs.
Enter your current rent and the yearly rent increase you expect.
Set the home appreciation rate and the investment return a renter could earn on the money saved.
Choose how many years you expect to stay, then read the verdict, the chart and the year-by-year table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Monthly cost to own = mortgage payment + (property tax + insurance + maintenance) ÷ 12
Buyer net worth = home value × (1 − selling cost %) − remaining loan balance
Renter net worth = down payment and buying closing costs invested, plus every month the owner's cost exceeds rent, all invested at your chosen return
Break-even year = first year in which buyer net worth is at least renter net worth
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Take a $450,000 home with 20% down. The down payment is $90,000, the loan is $360,000, and the 6.5% 30-year mortgage costs about $2,275 a month in principal and interest.

Step 2: Add ownership costs. Property tax at 1.1% is $4,950 a year ($412.50 a month), insurance is $1,800 a year ($150 a month) and maintenance at 1% of value is $4,500 a year ($375 a month). Total monthly cost to own in year one is about $3,213, compared with $2,400 in rent.

Step 3: Price the renter's savings. The renter keeps the $90,000 down payment and the $13,500 of buying closing costs (3% of the price), invested at 6%, for $103,500 at the start. Each month the owner spends $813 more than the renter pays in rent, and the renter invests that gap too.

Step 4: Read the result after 10 years, with 3% yearly appreciation and 3% rent increases. The owner's net worth after 6% selling costs is about $246,725. The renter's portfolio is about $287,225. Renting is ahead by $40,500, and the break-even year is not reached in this 10-year window. Extending the stay or changing the appreciation rate shows when the lines might cross.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Buying tends to win when you stay many years, because upfront and selling costs are spread across more years of equity growth.
High mortgage rates and a low rent-to-price ratio favor renting. Low rates, fast rent increases and strong local price growth favor buying.
Be honest about maintenance. Older homes often cost more than 1% of value each year, and a roof or furnace can cost a year's savings at once.
Test a pessimistic case with zero appreciation to see how much of the result depends on price growth rather than on the costs of ownership.
The renter's return assumes the saved money is invested every month. If you would spend the difference, the renter's position is much weaker.
This calculator does not model income tax deductions for mortgage interest or property tax, which matter only for households that itemize.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: Is it better to buy or rent a home?
default.a: Neither is always better. Buying usually pays off when you stay many years, can afford a sizeable down payment and the price is reasonable compared with rent in your area. Renting often wins for short stays, high prices, or when you can invest the savings well. Use this calculator with your own numbers rather than a rule of thumb.

default.q: What is the break-even point when buying vs renting?
default.a: It is the first year in which the owner's net worth (home equity after selling costs) is at least as large as the renter's investment portfolio. Before that year renting has been the cheaper path overall. If the break-even year is not reached within your time frame, renting was ahead for the whole period in these assumptions.

default.q: Does this calculator include tax deductions?
default.a: No. It does not model mortgage interest or property tax deductions, because many households take the standard deduction. Including deductions would make buying look somewhat better for households that itemize, so consult a tax professional if you do.

default.q: What investment return should I assume for the renter?
default.a: A long-run balanced stock and bond portfolio has historically returned roughly 5% to 7% a year before inflation. Use a lower number if the savings would sit in cash, and a higher number only if you accept the risk of large short-term losses.

default.q: Is a house a good investment?
default.a: A home gives you housing, forced savings through loan payments and possible appreciation, but it also carries ongoing costs and concentrates your wealth in one asset. Compare it with the alternatives here instead of assuming it always beats renting.

seo.title: Rental Property ROI Calculator: Cap Rate, Cash Flow & Cash-on-Cash
seo.description: Free rental property ROI calculator. Enter price, rent and expenses to get cap rate, cash-on-cash return, monthly cash flow, DSCR and break-even occupancy.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Check cap rate, cash-on-cash return, cash flow and debt coverage before you buy a rental.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A rental property can look attractive on a listing site and still lose money once taxes, insurance, repairs, vacancy and the mortgage are counted. Sellers and agents often quote the rent and leave out the costs, so the best test is to build the full annual income statement yourself before making an offer.

This rental property ROI calculator turns the purchase price, down payment, loan and expected rent into the figures investors and lenders actually use: net operating income, cap rate, monthly cash flow, cash-on-cash return on the money you put in, the debt service coverage ratio and the break-even occupancy. It also shows the gross rent multiplier and the 1% rule as quick screens.

Use the numbers to test the deal rather than to admire it. Small changes in rent, vacancy or the interest rate move cash flow a great deal when the down payment is small, because the loan payment is fixed and every dollar of lost rent comes straight out of the cash flow.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price, the down payment percentage and the closing costs.
Enter the loan rate and term, and the expected monthly rent.
Set a realistic vacancy rate, and add property tax, insurance, repairs and management fees.
Review net operating income, cash flow, cash-on-cash return and DSCR, then change one input at a time to stress-test the deal.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Net operating income (NOI) = collected rent − property tax − insurance − repairs − management
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
Cash flow = NOI − annual loan payments
Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow ÷ (down payment + closing costs)
DSCR = NOI ÷ annual loan payments
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Price and cash. A $300,000 duplex with 25% down is a $75,000 down payment. Closing costs at 3% add $9,000, so the cash invested is $84,000. The $225,000 loan at 6.75% over 30 years costs about $17,512 a year.

Step 2: Income. Rent of $2,500 a month is $30,000 a year. A 5% vacancy allowance removes $1,500, leaving $28,500 collected.

Step 3: Operating costs. Property tax is $3,600, insurance $1,500, repairs 5% of gross rent ($1,500) and management 8% of collected rent ($2,280). Together that is $8,880, so NOI is $28,500 minus $8,880, or $19,620.

Step 4: Returns. The cap rate is $19,620 ÷ $300,000, about 6.5%. Cash flow after the loan is $19,620 − $17,512 = $2,108 a year, which is $176 a month. Cash-on-cash return is $2,108 ÷ $84,000, about 2.5%. DSCR is $19,620 ÷ $17,512, about 1.12, which is below the 1.25 many lenders look for.

Step 5: Stress test. The calculator shows a break-even occupancy of about 87%. If occupancy falls below that level, the property no longer covers its costs and loan payment. This is the number to check against local vacancy rates.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Never assume zero vacancy or zero repairs. Even good tenants leave, and roofs, water heaters and appliances eventually need replacing.
Lenders usually want a DSCR of at least 1.2 to 1.25 for investment property loans, so a deal near 1.1 may be hard to finance.
Cap rate ignores financing, while cash-on-cash includes it. Look at both before you decide.
Check rent assumptions against current local listings rather than the seller's pro forma, which is often optimistic.
The 1% rule is a fast screen. Properties in high-tax or high-price areas often fail it but can still work with appreciation.
Add a capital reserve for big future costs, and remember that this calculator is before income tax and depreciation.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is a good ROI on a rental property?
default.a: Many investors target a cash-on-cash return of 8% or more and a cap rate at or above the local market average. What counts as good depends on risk, location, financing and your other options, so compare the deal with a simple index fund as well.

default.q: What is the difference between cap rate and cash-on-cash return?
default.a: Cap rate measures the property's income against its full price, as if you paid cash. Cash-on-cash return measures the cash flow you actually receive against the cash you invested, so it reflects your loan and down payment.

default.q: What expenses should I include?
default.a: Include property tax, insurance, a repair and maintenance reserve, management fees even if you manage the property yourself, vacancy, and any HOA dues or utilities you pay. Do not include loan principal in operating expenses, because principal is a way of building equity.

default.q: What is the 1% rule?
default.a: It is a rule of thumb that monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price. For a $300,000 property that means $3,000 a month. It is a quick screen, not a substitute for running the full numbers with expenses and financing.

default.q: What is debt service coverage ratio?
default.a: DSCR is net operating income divided by annual loan payments. A ratio of 1.0 means the property exactly covers its loan. Lenders typically want 1.2 to 1.25 or more, which leaves a cushion for vacancy and repairs.

seo.title: Real Estate ROI Calculator: Total Return with Appreciation
seo.description: Free real estate ROI calculator. Project cash flow, equity and appreciation over your holding period to see total ROI and annualized return on cash invested.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: See total return including cash flow, loan paydown and appreciation over your holding period.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Rental income is only one source of real estate returns. Over a multi-year hold you also build equity as the loan is paid down, and you benefit or suffer from changes in the property's value. A deal that barely covers its costs each month can still produce a strong total return once those other effects are added.

This calculator projects each year's cash flow, the loan balance, and the property's value with appreciation. It estimates your equity after selling costs, adds the cash flow you collected, and reports total ROI and the annualized return on the cash you put in. A year-by-year table shows where the return comes from.

Time matters. A 3% annual return looks modest, but compounded over ten years on a leveraged purchase it can add up to a large gain. The annualized figure lets you compare a property held for five years with one held for twelve, or with a stock index fund.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price, down payment, closing costs and loan terms.
Enter starting monthly rent, the expected yearly rent growth and the share of rent that goes to operating costs.
Set the appreciation rate, selling costs and the number of years you plan to hold the property.
Read total ROI, annualized return and the year-by-year projection of cash flow, equity and total position.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Equity at sale = sale price × (1 − selling cost %) − remaining loan balance
Total position = equity at sale + cumulative cash flow
Total ROI = (total position − cash invested) ÷ cash invested
Annualized return = (total position ÷ cash invested)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Cash invested. A $350,000 property with 20% down ($70,000) and 3% closing costs ($10,500) requires $80,500 of your money. The $280,000 loan is at 6.75% over 30 years.

Step 2: Early years. Rent starts at $2,600 a month, grows 3% a year, and 40% of rent goes to operating costs. After loan payments, year-one cash flow is about −$3,073, so you cover a small shortfall from your pocket. Cash flow turns positive in year seven, reaching about +$2,632 by year ten.

Step 3: Equity. With 3% annual appreciation, the property is worth about $470,000 after ten years. After 6% selling costs and the remaining loan balance, equity at sale is about $203,306.

Step 4: Total return. Adding the cumulative cash flow to equity gives a total position of about $199,981 against $80,500 invested. The profit is about $119,481, a total ROI of about 148%, or roughly 9.5% a year.

Step 5: Read the source of the return. Most of the gain comes from loan paydown and appreciation rather than from cash flow. That makes the result sensitive to the appreciation rate, so test a flat market before relying on the number.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use conservative appreciation. Long-run national averages are often quoted around 3% to 4%, but local markets can be flat or fall for years.
Leverage magnifies both gains and losses. Try a lower down payment to see how quickly a small price drop would wipe out your equity.
Negative early cash flow is a real cost. Make sure you can fund it for the years it lasts.
Selling costs are often 6% or more of the sale price once agent fees and transfer costs are included, so keep them in the model.
This calculator does not model income tax, depreciation recapture, capital gains or large capital repairs. Those can change the outcome a lot.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do you calculate ROI on real estate?
default.a: Add the property's cumulative cash flow to the equity you receive at sale, subtract the cash you originally invested, and divide by that cash. This calculator does it year by year so you can see how the return builds.

default.q: Is annualized return better than total ROI?
default.a: Annualized return lets you compare properties held for different lengths of time, and lets you compare real estate with other investments such as an index fund. Total ROI tells you the overall gain but not how fast it was earned.

default.q: Does the calculator include taxes?
default.a: No. Income tax, depreciation recapture and capital gains vary by situation, so consult a tax professional for after-tax results. Taxes can reduce the return considerably, especially when a property is sold.

default.q: Why is my cash flow negative in the early years?
default.a: Loan payments, taxes and insurance can exceed rent when you borrow heavily or buy at a high price. Rent growth and the falling loan balance usually improve cash flow over time, but the early shortfall is real money you must cover.

default.q: What holding period should I use?
default.a: Most investors test a range, such as five, seven and ten years, because the answer changes with timing. Short holds are more sensitive to selling costs, while longer holds give loan paydown and rent growth more time to work.

seo.title: Cap Rate Calculator: Capitalization Rate & Property Value
seo.description: Free cap rate calculator. Enter price, rent, vacancy and operating expenses to get NOI, capitalization rate, gross rent multiplier and value at the market cap rate.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Calculate capitalization rate and estimate what a property is worth at the market cap rate.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
The capitalization rate, or cap rate, is the annual net income a property produces as a percentage of its price. It ignores financing, which makes it useful for comparing properties of different sizes and prices, and for checking whether an asking price is in line with what similar buildings sell for.

This calculator builds net operating income from the monthly rent, a vacancy allowance and annual operating expenses, excluding loan payments. It then shows the cap rate of the property at its asking price, and the value that same income would support at a market cap rate you choose.

Cap rates are a snapshot of price against income, not a forecast. A low cap rate often means buyers expect strong growth or see low risk, while a high cap rate often means higher risk, weaker tenants or a weaker location. Treat the number as a starting point for a deeper look at the property.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price and the monthly gross rent.
Set a vacancy allowance and the annual operating expenses, leaving out loan payments.
Enter the cap rate that similar properties in the area are trading at.
Compare the property's cap rate with the market rate, and the implied value with the asking price.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Effective income = gross rent × 12 × (1 − vacancy)
NOI = effective income − operating expenses
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
Implied value = NOI ÷ market cap rate
Gross rent multiplier = purchase price ÷ annual gross rent
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Gross rent. A building priced at $800,000 collects $7,500 a month, which is $90,000 a year before any vacancy.

Step 2: Vacancy. A 5% allowance removes $4,500 of rent, leaving $85,500 of effective income.

Step 3: Operating costs. Taxes, insurance, repairs and management add up to $30,000 a year. Loan payments are not included, so NOI is $85,500 − $30,000 = $55,500.

Step 4: Cap rate. $55,500 ÷ $800,000 is about 6.94%. The gross rent multiplier is $800,000 ÷ $90,000, about 8.9.

Step 5: Compare with the market. If similar buildings trade at a 6% cap rate, the same income supports a value of $55,500 ÷ 0.06 = $925,000. That suggests the asking price is below the market value, assuming the rent and expense figures are reliable. The gap is a reason to verify the income, not a guarantee of a bargain.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Cap rate is only as reliable as the NOI behind it. Check rents against leases and expenses against tax bills and utility statements.
Higher cap rates usually mean higher risk or weaker locations, not simply a better deal. Compare like with like, such as similar property types in the same area.
Exclude mortgage payments, depreciation and income taxes from operating expenses. Include a reserve for repairs and capital replacement.
Vacancy allowances should reflect local conditions. A 5% allowance is common, but some markets need more and some need less.
Cap rate tells you about one year of income. It does not capture rent growth, lease terms or the condition of the building.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is a good cap rate?
default.a: It depends on the market, the property type and the risk. Many residential investors look for roughly 5% to 8%. Stable, high-demand areas often trade at lower cap rates, while riskier assets trade higher.

default.q: Does cap rate include the mortgage?
default.a: No. Cap rate assumes an all-cash purchase so that properties can be compared regardless of financing. Use cash-on-cash return to see the effect of a loan on your own return.

default.q: How do I value a property with its cap rate?
default.a: Divide net operating income by the market cap rate. That gives the price at which the property would match typical market returns for that type of asset and location.

default.q: What is the gross rent multiplier?
default.a: It is the price divided by annual gross rent, before expenses and vacancy. It is a quick comparison tool, and lower values generally mean a better price relative to rent.

default.q: Why is cap rate different from ROI?
default.a: Cap rate measures one year of income against price. ROI includes financing, appreciation and the full holding period, so it gives a broader view of what you earn.

seo.title: Cash on Cash Return Calculator for Rental Property
seo.description: Free cash on cash return calculator. See annual cash flow versus total cash invested, DSCR, and how rent changes of ±10% affect your return.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Measure annual cash flow against the cash you actually invest, then stress-test rent changes.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Cash-on-cash return answers a practical question: for every dollar of your own money in the deal, how many cents of cash flow do you get back each year? Because it counts only the cash you invested, it shows the effect of borrowing, which the cap rate hides.

This calculator adds up your down payment, closing costs and any upfront repair budget to find the cash you invested. It subtracts the loan payments from the net rental income to get annual cash flow, then reports the return, the debt service coverage ratio, and a sensitivity table showing how the return changes if rent moves up or down.

The sensitivity table is the most useful part for most investors. A small drop in rent can turn a modest positive return into a loss, and that risk is much larger when the down payment is small and the loan is large.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the price, the down payment percentage, the closing costs and any upfront repairs.
Enter the loan rate and term.
Enter monthly rent and the operating expenses as a percentage of rent.
Read the cash-on-cash return and DSCR, then use the sensitivity table to test lower and higher rent.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Cash invested = down payment + closing costs + upfront repairs
Annual cash flow = rent × 12 × (1 − expense ratio) − annual loan payments
Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow ÷ cash invested
DSCR = (rent × 12 × (1 − expense ratio)) ÷ annual loan payments
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Cash invested. A $275,000 rental with 25% down is $68,750. Closing costs at 3% are $8,250, and $5,000 of repairs brings the total cash invested to $82,000.

Step 2: Loan payments. The loan is $206,250 at 7% over 30 years, which costs about $1,372 a month or $16,466 a year.

Step 3: Net income. Rent of $2,400 a month is $28,800 a year. Operating expenses at 40% of rent take $11,520, leaving $17,280 of net income before the loan.

Step 4: Cash flow and return. $17,280 − $16,466 = $814 a year, about $68 a month. Divided by $82,000, that is a return of about 1.0%. DSCR is $17,280 ÷ $16,466, about 1.05. The return is positive but far below the common 8% target.

Step 5: Stress test. The sensitivity table shows that 10% less rent gives −$76 a month and a −1.1% return, while 10% more rent gives +$212 a month and about 3.1%. A rent change of only 10% moves the return by about 4 percentage points, which is why the calculator highlights rent as the key risk.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Include every dollar of cash you put in, including repairs, closing costs and any reserve you hold, not just the down payment.
An 8% to 12% cash-on-cash return is a common target, but risk and location matter as much as the number.
A very high return on a tiny cash investment can hide large risk, such as a thin down payment or aggressive rent assumptions. Check DSCR too.
Loan rates matter a lot. A one-point rate change can wipe out most of the cash flow on a leveraged purchase.
Vacancy is not in the expense ratio here, so either include it in the rent you enter or raise the expense percentage.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is cash on cash return?
default.a: It is annual pre-tax cash flow divided by the total cash you invested in the property. It focuses on the return on your own money rather than on the property's total value.

default.q: What is a good cash on cash return?
default.a: Many investors aim for 8% to 12%, though the right target depends on risk, market conditions and alternatives such as index funds or bonds. A return below your mortgage rate usually means the property is not adding cash flow.

default.q: How is it different from ROI?
default.a: Cash-on-cash return looks only at yearly cash flow on the cash you invested. Total ROI can also include appreciation and loan paydown over the whole holding period. Use the Real Estate ROI calculator for the broader view.

default.q: Why does a small rent change matter so much?
default.a: Loan payments are fixed, so every dollar of lost rent comes straight out of cash flow. The thinner your margin, the bigger the effect, which is why the sensitivity table is useful.

default.q: Should I include a vacancy allowance?
default.a: Yes. Either reduce the rent you enter by your expected vacancy or add the vacancy to your expense ratio. Leaving it out overstates the cash flow.

seo.title: Fix and Flip Calculator: Profit, ROI & 70% Rule Offer
seo.description: Free fix and flip calculator. Enter purchase price, rehab budget, ARV and financing to see net profit, return on cash invested and the 70% rule maximum offer.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate profit, return on cash and the 70% rule maximum offer before you buy a flip.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
House flipping margins are thinner than they look. Between the purchase, the rehab, loan interest and points, holding costs, and agent fees at sale, a deal that seems to leave $100,000 on paper can end up with a fraction of that. Time is the hidden cost: every extra month adds interest, taxes, insurance and utilities.

This calculator adds every cost, subtracts it from the after-repair value (ARV), and shows your net profit, the return on the cash you actually put in, and the maximum offer implied by the common 70% rule. It also shows how the result changes if the project runs longer than planned.

Most failed flips come from one of three things: an ARV that was too optimistic, a rehab that ran over budget, or a timeline that doubled. The calculator makes all three visible before you commit money, so you can test the deal against slower and more expensive scenarios.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price, the rehab budget and the ARV based on recent comparable sales.
Set how many months you expect the project to take from closing to sale.
Enter the loan terms: percent financed, interest rate and points. Use 0% financed for an all-cash flip.
Enter buying closing costs, monthly holding costs and selling costs.
Check the profit, the return and the 70% rule offer, then test a longer timeline or a higher rehab cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Total cost = purchase + rehab + buying costs + loan interest + points + holding costs + selling costs
Net profit = ARV − total cost
Return on cash = net profit ÷ cash you invested
70% rule maximum offer = ARV × 70% − rehab cost
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Set the deal. You buy at $200,000, spend $45,000 on rehab and expect an ARV of $330,000 after six months. The lender finances 80% of the purchase, which is $160,000, at 11% with 2 points.

Step 2: Financing. Interest is $160,000 × 11% × 6/12 = $8,800, and the points are $3,200, so financing costs $12,000. Buying closing costs at 2% add $4,000.

Step 3: Holding and selling. Holding costs of $1,200 a month for six months are $7,200, bringing holding and closing costs to $11,200. Selling costs at 7% of $330,000 are $23,100.

Step 4: Profit and return. Total costs are $200,000 + $45,000 + $12,000 + $11,200 + $23,100 = $291,300. Profit is $330,000 − $291,300 = $38,700. Your cash is $40,000 down, $45,000 of rehab, $11,200 of holding and closing costs and $12,000 of financing costs, or $108,200, so the return is about 36%.

Step 5: Timeline risk. Stretch the same project to nine months and holding costs rise to $10,800, interest and points to $16,400, and profit falls to about $30,700 on $116,200 of cash, a 26% return. The 70% rule suggests an offer of no more than $186,000 for this ARV and rehab.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Be conservative with ARV. Use sold comparables within a mile and from the last six months, not listing prices or optimistic estimates.
Add a contingency of 10% to 15% to the rehab budget. Hidden damage, permits and material price rises are normal.
Every extra month adds interest, taxes, insurance and utilities. Test slower timelines before you commit to a loan with a short term.
Hard money lenders often charge points and extension fees. Check what happens if the project runs late.
The 70% rule is a screen, not a guarantee. In expensive markets investors may accept a higher percentage, and in weak markets a lower one.
Profit from a flip is usually taxed as ordinary income in the US if held under a year, so the after-tax result is lower than this estimate.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is the 70% rule in house flipping?
default.a: It says an investor should pay no more than 70% of the after-repair value minus the cost of repairs. For an ARV of $300,000 and $40,000 of repairs, the maximum offer is $170,000.

default.q: How much profit should a flip make?
default.a: Many investors look for at least $25,000 to $30,000 of profit or a 15% to 20% return on cash per project, because flips carry risk of delays, cost overruns and price drops.

default.q: What costs do people forget when flipping?
default.a: Loan points and interest, holding costs such as utilities and insurance, permits, dumpsters, staging and the seller's closing costs are commonly underestimated.

default.q: Why does the timeline matter so much?
default.a: Interest, holding costs and points keep running while the house sits. A three-month delay on a loan with monthly interest can cost as much as a bad negotiation.

default.q: Does this include taxes on the profit?
default.a: No. Flip profits are often taxed as ordinary income when held for a short time. Talk to a tax professional about your situation before you buy.

seo.title: Closing Costs Calculator: Estimate Cash Needed to Close
seo.description: Free closing costs calculator for home buyers. Estimate lender fees, title and escrow, inspection, transfer taxes and prepaids to see total cash to close.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate lender fees, title charges and prepaid items to see how much cash you need at closing.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Many first-time buyers save hard for the down payment and are surprised by closing costs on top of it. These are the fees and prepaid items due when the sale completes. They commonly run between 2% and 5% of the home price, and they are often paid in cash on closing day.

This calculator breaks them into lender fees, title and escrow, appraisal and inspection, recording and transfer taxes, and prepaid property tax and insurance. It adds your down payment to show the total cash to close, which is the figure to plan for.

The numbers are estimates. Your Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure show the real charges, and the state, lender and loan type all change the result. Use this tool to plan early and to see which items you can negotiate or shop for.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the home price and your planned down payment percentage.
Adjust lender fees, title and escrow, and recording and transfer percentages using your Loan Estimate.
Add the appraisal and inspection costs.
Enter annual property tax and insurance, and how many months of each your lender will collect upfront.
Read the total closing costs and the cash you need at closing.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Lender fees = loan amount × lender fee %
Title and escrow = home price × title %
Prepaids = (annual tax + annual insurance) ÷ 12 × prepaid months
Cash to close = down payment + all closing costs
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Loan and down payment. A $400,000 home with 10% down needs a $40,000 down payment, leaving a $360,000 loan.

Step 2: Lender and title. A 1% lender fee on the loan is $3,600. Title and escrow at 0.8% of the price is $3,200.

Step 3: Third-party and government charges. The appraisal and inspection cost $1,000, and recording and transfer charges at 0.4% of the price are $1,600.

Step 4: Prepaids. Annual property tax of $4,400 and insurance of $1,800 total $6,200. Six months of prepaids is $3,100, which funds your first tax and insurance bills.

Step 5: Totals. Closing costs add up to $12,500, about 3.1% of the price. With the $40,000 down payment, you should plan to bring about $52,500 to closing.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Your lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days of applying. Use its numbers for the most accurate figures.
Transfer taxes and title insurance rates differ a lot by state, and some states charge large transfer taxes to buyers.
You can sometimes negotiate seller credits, or ask for a lender credit in exchange for a slightly higher rate.
Shop for title and settlement services. Compare the fees on the Loan Estimate for lender, title and escrow.
Prepaid items are not extra expenses in the long run. They fund your first tax and insurance bills, so the cash comes back over the year.
Keep a reserve after closing. Moving, repairs and furniture costs often arrive in the first few months.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much are closing costs on a house?
default.a: Buyers typically pay about 2% to 5% of the purchase price. The exact amount depends on the state, lender, loan type, and whether you buy discount points.

default.q: Are closing costs included in the down payment?
default.a: No. The down payment goes toward the price of the home. Closing costs are paid separately, unless you negotiate seller credits or roll some costs into certain loans.

default.q: Who pays closing costs, the buyer or the seller?
default.a: Both pay some costs. Buyers usually pay lender, title and prepaid items. Sellers typically pay agent commissions and some transfer charges, depending on local custom and negotiation.

default.q: Can I reduce my closing costs?
default.a: Yes. Compare lenders, ask about fee waivers, shop for title and insurance, negotiate seller concessions, and avoid buying discount points if you may sell soon.

default.q: What are prepaids at closing?
default.a: Prepaids are advance payments for property tax and homeowners insurance, which the lender collects into an escrow account. They are part of your cash to close but fund future bills.

seo.title: Commercial NOI Calculator: Net Operating Income & DSCR
seo.description: Free commercial NOI calculator. Enter rent, vacancy and operating expenses to calculate net operating income, expense ratio, cap rate and debt service coverage.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Build a simple income statement for an income property and see NOI, cap rate and debt coverage.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Net operating income is the number that drives commercial property value and loan approval. It is the income a property produces after vacancy and operating expenses, but before the mortgage, depreciation and income taxes. Lenders and buyers use it to judge how much a building is worth and how much debt it can carry.

This calculator builds a simple annual income statement from rent, other income and your expense lines. It reports NOI, the expense ratio, the cap rate on your purchase price, and the debt service coverage ratio that lenders review before approving a loan.

Commercial numbers are only as good as their inputs. Sellers often show rent that is not fully collected and expenses that exclude real costs, so check each line against leases, bills and the operating history before you rely on the result.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the scheduled monthly rent and any other income, such as parking, laundry or signage.
Set a vacancy and credit loss percentage.
Enter annual property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance, and a management percentage of income.
Add the purchase price and loan terms to see the cap rate and debt coverage.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Gross potential income = (rent + other income) × 12
Effective gross income = gross potential income × (1 − vacancy)
NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
DSCR = NOI ÷ annual loan payments
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Income. Monthly rent of $24,000 plus $1,200 of other income is $25,200 a month, or $302,400 a year before vacancy.

Step 2: Vacancy. A 7% vacancy and credit loss removes $21,168, leaving effective gross income of $281,232.

Step 3: Expenses. Property tax is $28,000, insurance $9,000, utilities $12,000 and repairs $18,000. Management at 5% of effective income is $14,062. Total operating expenses are about $81,062, an expense ratio of about 29%.

Step 4: NOI and cap rate. $281,232 − $81,062 = $200,170 of NOI. On a $2.8 million price, that is a cap rate of about 7.15%.

Step 5: Debt coverage. With a 70% loan of $1.96 million at 6.75% over 25 years, annual loan payments are about $162,700. DSCR is $200,170 ÷ $162,700, about 1.23. That is just under the 1.25 many lenders want, so a lender might offer a smaller loan.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Do not include mortgage payments, depreciation or income tax in operating expenses. Those are below the NOI line.
Use the seller's operating statements, then verify them against tax bills, utility bills and the rent roll and leases.
Include a repair and capital reserve, even if the seller does not. Roofs, parking lots and HVAC systems are large costs in commercial property.
Compare the expense ratio with similar buildings. A very low ratio can mean costs are missing.
Lenders may size the loan from DSCR rather than from value, so a small change in NOI can change how much you can borrow.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is NOI in real estate?
default.a: Net operating income is a property's income after vacancy and operating expenses, but before debt service, depreciation and income taxes. It describes the building itself, rather than the financing.

default.q: Is NOI the same as cash flow?
default.a: No. Cash flow is what remains after paying the loan. NOI is calculated before loan payments, so it shows the value of the property independent of how it is financed.

default.q: What is a good DSCR?
default.a: Lenders often require 1.20 to 1.35 for commercial loans. A higher ratio gives more cushion above the loan payments if vacancy rises or costs increase.

default.q: What is a normal expense ratio?
default.a: It varies by property type. Many multifamily properties run between about 35% and 50% of effective income, while a triple-net lease shifts most costs to the tenant and has a much lower ratio.

default.q: Why does vacancy matter so much?
default.a: Vacancy reduces income while many costs stay fixed, so a few percentage points of extra vacancy can cut NOI noticeably and push DSCR below a lender's minimum.

seo.title: Property Tax Calculator: Annual & Monthly Estimate With Forecast
seo.description: Free property tax calculator. Enter home value, tax rate and exemptions to estimate annual and monthly property tax and project it over 1 to 30 years.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate your annual and monthly property tax and see how it could grow over the years.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Property tax is one of the largest ongoing costs of owning a home, and it varies enormously by location. Effective rates range from well under 1% of value in some areas to above 2% in several high-tax places, which can mean thousands of dollars a year on two homes of the same price.

This calculator multiplies the taxable value of a home by your local effective rate, subtracts any exemptions, and gives the annual and monthly bill. It then projects how the bill could change if the assessed value keeps rising, which is common in growing areas.

The effective rate matters more than the headline millage rate. Local tax authorities set rates on assessed values that may not match market value, so the most reliable input is last year's tax bill divided by the home's market value. Tax bills can also include separate charges, such as special district levies and bond assessments, which are not always part of the headline rate. Add up every line on the bill before dividing by the value, so the calculation matches what you will actually pay.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the home's assessed or market value.
Enter the effective tax rate from your county tax bill or assessor's website.
Add any exemptions that reduce taxable value, such as a homestead exemption.
Set how fast the assessed value is expected to rise and how many years to project.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Taxable value = home value − exemptions
Annual property tax = taxable value × effective tax rate
Monthly property tax = annual tax ÷ 12
Future annual tax = current tax × (1 + annual growth)^years
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Taxable value. A $400,000 home with a $0 exemption has a taxable value of $400,000.

Step 2: Annual bill. At an effective rate of 1.1%, the bill is $4,400 a year, or $367 a month.

Step 3: Growth. If assessed value rises 3% a year, the bill is $4,532 in year two, $4,952 in year five and about $5,741 by year ten. The total paid over the ten years is about $50,441.

Step 4: Exemption. A $50,000 homestead exemption reduces taxable value to $350,000, which lowers the starting bill by $550 a year at a 1.1% rate.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use the effective rate (tax divided by market value), not the nominal millage rate, unless you convert it correctly.
In some states a sale triggers a reassessment at the purchase price, so the previous owner's bill can understate yours.
Check the exemptions you qualify for, such as homestead, senior or veteran exemptions, and appeal the assessment if it looks too high.
Escrow accounts collect property tax monthly with your mortgage payment, so the bill still affects the total you pay each month.
Special assessments for local projects are often billed separately and are not included in this estimate.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How is property tax calculated?
default.a: Local governments multiply the taxable value of a property by the combined rate set by counties, cities and school districts, after exemptions are subtracted.

default.q: What is an effective property tax rate?
default.a: It is the annual tax bill divided by the home's market value. It makes areas comparable even when assessment methods and tax rates differ.

default.q: Can I lower my property tax?
default.a: Often yes. Apply for any exemptions you qualify for, and appeal the assessment if you believe it exceeds market value, following your county's deadline.

default.q: Why did my property tax go up?
default.a: Common reasons are a higher assessed value, new voter-approved levies, the end of a temporary exemption, or a reassessment after a sale or major renovation.

default.q: Is property tax deductible?
default.a: In the US, property tax can be deducted on federal returns for those who itemize, subject to limits. Check the current rules with a tax professional.

seo.title: Hard Money Loan Calculator: Interest, Points & True Cost
seo.description: Free hard money loan calculator. Enter loan amount, rate, points and term to see monthly interest, total cost and the effective annual cost of the loan.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: See the true cost of a short-term hard money loan, including points, interest and fees.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Hard money loans are short-term, asset-based loans often used by investors to buy and renovate properties. They can close quickly, based mostly on the value of the property rather than the borrower's income, but they cost more than a bank mortgage because lenders charge higher interest and upfront points.

This calculator shows your interest-only monthly payment and adds up the interest, points and fees over the term you choose. It converts the total into an effective annual cost, so you can compare the loan with other financing, and it shows loan-to-value at payoff.

The effective annual cost is the number to watch. Points and fees are paid once, so a short loan has a much higher annual cost than a long one, even if the interest rate is the same.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the loan amount, the interest rate and the points.
Set the loan term in months and add any other lender or closing fees.
Enter the expected value of the property at payoff to see the loan-to-value ratio.
Review the monthly payment, the total cost, and how the cost changes if the project runs longer.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Monthly interest = loan × annual rate ÷ 12
Total cost = monthly interest × months + points + fees
Effective annual cost = total cost ÷ loan ÷ (months ÷ 12)
Loan to value = loan ÷ value at payoff
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Monthly interest. A $250,000 loan at 11.5% costs $250,000 × 11.5% ÷ 12 = $2,396 a month.

Step 2: Twelve-month total. Interest for 12 months is $28,750. Points at 2% add $5,000, and other fees add $2,500, for a total cost of $36,250.

Step 3: Effective annual cost. $36,250 ÷ $250,000 is about 14.5% for one year, which is the figure to compare with other financing.

Step 4: Shorter loan. The same points and fees on a three-month term give a total cost of about $14,688, or about 23.5% a year. A six-month term costs about $21,875, or about 17.5% a year.

Step 5: Risk. A project that takes 18 months instead of 12 adds about $14,000 of interest. Loan-to-value at payoff is $250,000 ÷ $400,000, about 63%, which gives the lender a cushion.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Points are paid upfront and weigh more heavily on short loans. Compare the effective annual cost, not just the rate.
Ask about extension fees, minimum interest periods, draw inspection charges and prepayment penalties.
Have a clear exit plan, such as a sale or a refinance into long-term financing, and know how long it will take.
Compare several lenders. Rates and points differ meaningfully, and some lenders are more flexible about extensions.
Hard money loans are often secured by the property, so a missed payment can lead to foreclosure.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What are typical hard money loan rates?
default.a: Rates commonly run roughly 9% to 15% with 1 to 4 points, depending on the lender, the borrower's experience and the deal. Check current offers from several lenders.

default.q: Are hard money loans interest-only?
default.a: Usually. You pay interest each month and repay the principal as a balloon payment when you sell or refinance.

default.q: How is a hard money loan different from a bank loan?
default.a: It is based mostly on the property's value rather than the borrower's income, closes faster, has a short term and costs more. It is designed for investors with a clear exit, not for a long-term home loan.

default.q: Why is the effective annual cost higher than the rate?
default.a: Points and fees are charged once, on top of the interest. When spread over a year, they add to the annual rate, and the effect is largest on the shortest loans.

default.q: What happens if the project runs late?
default.a: Interest keeps accruing and extension fees may apply. Use the calculator to test a longer term before you borrow, so you know the cost of a delay.

seo.title: Refinance Calculator: Break-Even Point & Monthly Savings
seo.description: Free mortgage refinance calculator. Compare your current loan with a new one to see monthly savings, break-even months and net savings after closing costs.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Find your monthly savings, break-even point and net savings from refinancing your mortgage.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Refinancing replaces your mortgage with a new one. It can lower the monthly payment, shorten the loan or change its type, but it comes with closing costs. Whether it pays off depends on how much you save each month and how long you keep the new loan.

This calculator compares your current loan with a new one. It reports the new payment, the monthly savings, the number of months needed to recover the closing costs, and the net savings over the number of years you expect to keep the loan.

A common mistake is to focus on the monthly payment alone. A new 30-year loan lowers the payment but restarts the clock, so the calculator also shows the year-by-year net savings. That lets you see whether the lower payment is a real saving or simply more interest over time.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your current loan balance, interest rate and years remaining.
Enter the new rate, the new term and the refinance closing costs.
Set how long you expect to keep the loan.
Compare monthly savings, break-even months and net savings over time.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Monthly savings = current payment − new payment
Break-even months = closing costs ÷ monthly savings
Net savings after N years = cumulative payments saved − closing costs
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Starting point. Your balance is $320,000 at 7.25% with 27 years left on the loan.

Step 2: New loan. You refinance into a new 30-year loan at 6.25% and pay $6,000 in closing costs. The new loan restarts the term, which is why the payment falls.

Step 3: Monthly saving. The payment falls by about $283 a month, which is the figure used for the break-even calculation.

Step 4: Break-even. $6,000 ÷ $283 means you recover the closing costs after about 22 months. Year one is a net loss of about $2,824, and by the end of year two the savings are ahead, at about $295.

Step 5: Seven-year result. If you keep the loan for seven years, the net savings are about $14,783. Restarting the 30-year clock adds years of interest, so compare the total interest with a 20-year option before you decide.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Restarting a 30-year clock lowers the payment but can raise lifetime interest. Compare the total cost, not only the monthly payment.
If you may move before the break-even point, refinancing may not pay off. Check how long you realistically plan to stay.
A no-closing-cost loan usually has a higher rate. Compare the total cost of that option with paying the costs upfront.
Get written Loan Estimates from several lenders so the fees are comparable.
Cash-out refinances add to your balance and change the break-even math, so run them separately.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: When does refinancing make sense?
default.a: When you will keep the loan well past the break-even point and the savings or a shorter term meet your goals. A rate drop of about one percentage point is a common rule of thumb, but run your own numbers.

default.q: How long does it take to break even on a refinance?
default.a: Divide the closing costs by the monthly savings. With $6,000 of costs and about $283 of monthly savings, break-even takes about 22 months.

default.q: Does refinancing hurt my credit score?
default.a: A lender's credit check can cause a small, temporary dip, and a new account changes your credit mix. The effect is usually modest and fades over time.

default.q: Should I choose a shorter term?
default.a: A shorter term has a higher payment but saves interest and builds equity faster. Choose based on a payment you can comfortably afford for the whole term.

default.q: Are closing costs included in the loan?
default.a: They can be paid upfront or rolled into the loan. Rolling them in lowers the cash you need but increases the balance and the total interest.

seo.title: Home Equity Calculator: How Much Can You Borrow?
seo.description: Free home equity calculator. Enter home value and mortgage balance to see equity, loan-to-value, available borrowing and estimated HELOC or home equity loan payments.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out your home equity, how much you can borrow and what a HELOC would cost per month.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Home equity is the part of your home's value that you own: its market value minus what you still owe. Lenders let you borrow against it with a home equity loan or a line of credit (HELOC), but they limit total borrowing to a share of the home's value, which leaves a cushion for falling prices.

This calculator shows your equity and current loan-to-value, estimates how much you could borrow under a combined loan-to-value limit, and estimates the monthly payment on the amount you choose, both as interest-only and as a fully repaying loan.

Borrowing against the home puts the home at risk if payments are missed. The best use of equity is usually a purpose that adds value, such as repairs, and the calculator helps you test how much debt the home can carry before the payment becomes a strain. Compare the cost of borrowing against equity with other options, such as a personal loan or a cash-out refinance, because fees, rates and terms differ. Before you borrow, work out the monthly payment on your full household budget, including a possible rate rise on a variable-rate line.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the home's current value and your mortgage balance.
Set the maximum combined loan-to-value your lender allows.
Enter the amount you want to borrow, the rate and the repayment period.
Check the available amount, the payment and how much equity remains.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Equity = home value − mortgage balance
Maximum total borrowing = home value × combined LTV limit
Available to borrow = maximum total borrowing − mortgage balance
Payment = standard amortized payment on the amount borrowed
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Equity. A $500,000 home with a $290,000 mortgage has $210,000 of equity, and a current loan-to-value of 58%.

Step 2: Borrowing limit. At an 85% combined limit, total debt on the home can reach $425,000. Subtract the $290,000 mortgage and about $135,000 is available.

Step 3: Payment. Borrowing $60,000 at 8.5% costs $425 a month if you pay only interest. Repaying it over 15 years costs about $591 a month.

Step 4: Position after borrowing. Total debt becomes $350,000, or 70% of the home's value, and $150,000 of equity remains.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Your home is collateral. Missed payments can put it at risk, so only borrow what you can repay comfortably.
Home values are estimates until an appraisal. Be conservative, because a price drop can reduce your borrowing power.
Many HELOCs have variable rates, so payments can rise. Test a higher rate before you borrow.
Interest-only payments keep the balance unchanged, so you must plan for the repayment period when it starts.
Interest on home equity debt may be tax deductible in some cases if the money is used to buy, build or improve the home. Check current rules.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do I calculate home equity?
default.a: Subtract everything you owe on the home from its current market value. If it is worth $500,000 and you owe $290,000, your equity is $210,000.

default.q: What is a combined loan-to-value (CLTV) ratio?
default.a: It is all loans secured by the home divided by the home's value. Lenders often cap it around 80% to 90%, depending on credit score and the property.

default.q: What is the difference between a HELOC and a home equity loan?
default.a: A home equity loan gives a lump sum with fixed payments. A HELOC is a revolving line of credit, usually with a variable rate, a draw period and then a repayment period.

default.q: Does borrowing against equity reduce my equity?
default.a: Yes. Every dollar you borrow lowers the equity in the home by the same amount, though regular repayments gradually restore it.

default.q: How much equity should I keep?
default.a: Many homeowners keep at least 15% to 20% of the home's value as equity, which leaves room for falling prices and unexpected costs.

seo.title: Gravel Calculator: Cubic Yards, Tons & Cost
seo.description: Free gravel calculator. Enter length, width and depth to get cubic yards, tons, bags and estimated cost, with an editable material weight and price.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out how many cubic yards, tons and bags of gravel you need for any rectangular area.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Ordering the right amount of gravel saves a second delivery fee and a half-finished project. Suppliers sell gravel by the ton or the cubic yard, but most people measure a project in feet and inches, so a conversion is needed before you can place the order. Getting that conversion wrong is the most common reason for a shortfall.

This calculator turns the length, width and depth of your area into cubic feet, cubic yards and tons, and it also gives the number of 0.5 cubic foot bags for small jobs. It adds an allowance for settling and compaction, then estimates the cost from the delivered price per ton that you enter.

Depth is the input that changes the answer most. A path that is two inches deep needs a fraction of the material of a driveway that is four inches deep, so decide on the finished depth before you measure. The depth table on the page shows the same area at several depths so you can compare options quickly.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Measure the length and width of the area in feet.
Enter the depth in inches. Paths often use 2 to 3 inches, and driveways commonly use 4 to 8 inches built in layers.
Adjust the material weight if your supplier gives a different figure per cubic yard.
Enter the delivered price per ton to see the estimated cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Cubic feet = length (ft) × width (ft) × depth (in) ÷ 12
Cubic yards = cubic feet ÷ 27, plus an allowance for settling
Tons = cubic yards × material weight (about 1.4 tons per yard for gravel)
Bags (0.5 cubic foot) = cubic feet ÷ 0.5
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Volume. A 20 ft by 10 ft area is 200 square feet. Three inches of depth is 0.25 feet, so the volume is 200 × 0.25 = 50 cubic feet.

Step 2: Cubic yards and settling. 50 cubic feet ÷ 27 is about 1.85 cubic yards. Adding a 5% allowance for settling gives about 1.94 cubic yards.

Step 3: Tons. At 1.4 tons per cubic yard, 1.94 yards is about 2.72 tons.

Step 4: Cost. At $40 a ton the material costs about $109. The depth table shows the same area at 1 inch (about 0.65 cubic yards, $36) and 2 inches (about 1.3 cubic yards, $73), which helps you choose.

seo.title: Gravel Driveway Calculator: Tons, Layers & Cost
seo.description: Free gravel driveway calculator. Enter length, width and layer depths to estimate tons of base and surface stone, cubic yards, delivery and total cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate base and surface stone, tons and cost for a new or refreshed gravel driveway.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A durable gravel driveway is built in layers: a coarse base for strength and drainage, and a finer surface layer that locks together under traffic. Each layer needs a different stone and quantity, so a single depth estimate often leads to under-ordering or to the wrong product.

This calculator works out both layers from the driveway's size and your chosen depths, adds an allowance for compaction, and totals the cost of the two stones and delivery. It also reports the cost per square foot, which makes it easier to compare quotes from different suppliers.

A driveway fails most often because of water, not thickness. The surface needs a slight crown and a ditch or drain on each side, and the base must be well compacted. The calculator gives the quantities, but the build quality decides how long the driveway lasts.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length and width of the driveway in feet.
Set the base layer depth and the surface layer depth in inches.
Add an allowance for compaction, typically 10% to 20%.
Enter the price per ton for each stone and your delivery charge to see the total.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Layer cubic yards = length × width × depth (in) ÷ 12 ÷ 27 × (1 + compaction)
Layer tons = cubic yards × material weight
Total cost = base cost + surface cost + delivery
Cost per square foot = total cost ÷ (length × width)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Area. A 60 ft by 12 ft driveway is 720 square feet.

Step 2: Base layer. A 4 inch base is 720 × 4 ÷ 12 = 240 cubic feet, or 8.9 cubic yards. With a 15% compaction allowance it is about 10.2 cubic yards, or 14.3 tons at 1.4 tons per yard.

Step 3: Surface layer. A 2 inch surface is 120 cubic feet, or 4.4 cubic yards. With the same allowance it is about 5.1 cubic yards, or 7.2 tons.

Step 4: Cost. Base stone at $35 a ton costs about $501, surface stone at $42 a ton costs about $301, and delivery adds $150. The total is about $951, or $1.32 per square foot.

Step 5: Check. The whole driveway needs about 21.5 tons. If you ordered only the surface quantity, you would have a thin, unstable road that would soon need rebuilding.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Good drainage matters more than thickness. Crown the driveway, use ditches on both sides and keep water from pooling at the entrance.
A geotextile fabric under the base helps on soft soil and keeps the stone layers from mixing into the ground.
Expect to top up the surface every few years as stone migrates and ruts form, especially where cars turn or brake.
Order the base first and compact it in lifts. Adding surface stone to an uncompacted base wastes material.
Delivery charges can be a large share of a small order, so ask for a single delivery rather than several smaller loads.

default.a: A common build uses larger base stone, such as 2 to 3 inch crushed stone, and a smaller angular surface stone such as crusher run or 3/4 inch minus that compacts firmly. Local suppliers will recommend what works in your soil.

default.q: How thick should a gravel driveway be?
default.a: Most are 6 to 8 inches thick in total, built in two or three compacted layers. Soft soil or heavy vehicles call for more.

default.q: Why order extra gravel for a driveway?
default.a: Loose stone compacts when rolled and some is lost into the subsoil, so adding 10% to 20% avoids a shortfall at the end of the job.

default.q: How often does a gravel driveway need more stone?
default.a: Many driveways need a light top-up every two to five years, depending on traffic, rainfall and how well the base was built.

seo.title: French Drain Calculator: Gravel, Pipe & Fabric Needed
seo.description: Free French drain calculator. Enter trench length, width, depth and pipe size to estimate tons of gravel, feet of pipe, filter fabric and materials cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Calculate gravel, pipe, filter fabric and cost for a French drain of any length.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A French drain moves groundwater away from a foundation or a soggy yard using a gravel-filled trench with a perforated pipe inside. It works only if the materials are right and the trench slopes toward a proper outlet. The three main purchases, pipe, clean gravel and filter fabric, are each sized from the trench.

This calculator subtracts the volume of the pipe from the trench, so you do not over-order gravel. It works out how much pipe you need, adds a small allowance for cuts, and calculates the fabric needed to wrap the stone around the whole trench with an overlap. It then totals the materials at the prices you enter.

Length, width and depth decide the cost. Deeper trenches intercept more water but need more digging, more gravel and more fabric. Before you buy, confirm the outlet location, because a drain that discharges onto a neighbor's land or into a low spot can create a bigger problem.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length of the drain, and the trench width and depth in inches.
Choose the pipe diameter, usually 4 inches for residential drains.
Add a small waste allowance for extra pipe and gravel.
Enter local prices for gravel, pipe and fabric to see the materials cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Trench volume = length × width × depth
Pipe volume = π × (pipe radius)² × length
Gravel volume = (trench volume − pipe volume) × (1 + waste)
Fabric = length × (2 × depth + width + 12 in overlap)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Trench volume. A 50 ft drain that is 12 inches (1 ft) wide and 24 inches (2 ft) deep has a trench of 50 × 1 × 2 = 100 cubic feet.

Step 2: Subtract the pipe. A 4 inch pipe takes about 4.4 cubic feet over 50 feet, so the gravel space is about 95.6 cubic feet.

Step 3: Add waste and convert. A 10% allowance makes it about 105 cubic feet, or 3.9 cubic yards. At 1.4 tons per yard that is about 5.5 tons of gravel.

Step 4: Pipe and fabric. Pipe at 10% extra is 55 feet. Fabric is 50 × (2 × 2 + 1 + 1) = 330 square feet, wrapping the stone with an overlap.

Step 5: Cost. At the default prices, gravel is about $245, pipe about $138 and fabric about $99, so the materials cost about $482 before digging or disposal.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Slope the trench about 1% (one inch of fall every eight feet) toward a safe outlet, and keep the slope continuous.
Use clean washed stone, and place the perforated pipe with the holes facing down so water enters from the bottom.
Wrap the stone, not the pipe, with filter fabric to keep silt out while letting water in.
Check where the water will exit. Do not drain onto a neighbor's land, and check local rules about discharging to storm drains.
Call 811 before you dig to find buried utilities, which often run close to the surface near homes.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much gravel do I need for a French drain?
default.a: Multiply trench length, width and depth to get cubic feet, subtract the pipe volume, and convert to cubic yards and tons. The calculator does this and adds an allowance for settling.

default.q: How deep should a French drain be?
default.a: Often 18 to 36 inches. It should be deep enough to catch the water you want to remove, with a continuous slope down to the outlet.

default.q: What size pipe should I use?
default.a: Four-inch perforated pipe is the common choice for residential drains. Larger pipe can be used for long runs or heavy flows, but it costs more and needs more gravel.

default.q: Does a French drain need filter fabric?
default.a: In most soils, yes. Fabric keeps fine soil from clogging the stone and pipe over time, which is the most common reason a drain stops working.

default.q: Can a French drain go in a wet area all year?
default.a: It works best where the water table is below the trench. If the ground stays saturated, the drain may only move water slowly, and a larger system or a different solution may be needed.

seo.title: Retaining Wall Block Calculator: Blocks, Caps & Gravel
seo.description: Free retaining wall block calculator. Enter wall length, height and block size to estimate wall blocks, cap blocks, backfill gravel and materials cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate wall blocks, cap blocks, drainage gravel and materials cost for a segmental retaining wall.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A segmental retaining wall is built from stacked interlocking blocks on a compacted gravel base, with drainage gravel behind it. The block count depends on both the wall's size and the face dimensions of the block you choose, and most mistakes come from miscounting courses or forgetting the buried base.

This calculator counts the visible courses plus any buried courses, works out the blocks per course from the wall length, adds cap blocks and a waste allowance for cuts, and estimates the base and backfill gravel and the materials cost. It shows the visible face area so you can check the scale of the wall.

Height is the factor that carries the most risk. Walls taller than the limits in local codes need engineered designs and permits, and water pressure behind the wall is the usual reason a wall fails. Use the calculator for quantities, then confirm the design with your building department or an engineer.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the wall length and the visible height in feet.
Enter the face width and height of your block, and the length of the cap block, in inches.
Set the number of buried base courses and an allowance for cuts.
Enter the gravel backfill and base dimensions, and the unit prices.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Courses = ceil(visible height × 12 ÷ block height) + buried courses
Blocks per course = ceil(length × 12 ÷ block width)
Wall blocks = courses × blocks per course × (1 + waste)
Gravel = (length × height × backfill width) + (length × base width × base depth)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Courses. A 3 ft wall with 6 inch blocks has 3 × 12 ÷ 6 = 6 visible courses, plus 1 buried course, for 7 in total.

Step 2: Blocks per course. A 30 ft wall with 16 inch blocks needs 30 × 12 ÷ 16 = 22.5, which rounds up to 23 blocks per course.

Step 3: Wall blocks. 7 courses × 23 blocks is 161, plus 8% for cuts, gives 174 blocks.

Step 4: Cap blocks. A 12 inch cap covers 12 inches of wall, so a 30 ft wall needs 30 caps. The waste allowance applies to wall blocks only.

Step 5: Gravel and cost. The backfill and base need about 4.4 cubic yards, or 6.2 tons, of gravel. At the default prices, blocks cost about $783, caps $120 and gravel $280, a total of about $1,183.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Many codes require a permit and an engineer for walls above about 4 feet, measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall. Some places set the limit lower, and walls supporting a slope, driveway or building often need engineering at any height.
Always add drainage gravel and a perforated drain pipe behind the wall. Water pressure is the main cause of retaining wall failures.
Buy a few extra blocks from the same production lot to avoid colour differences between batches.
Lay the first course level and compact the base. A poor first course causes every course above it to misalign.
Plan the cap placement early. Caps are glued in place and hide the hollow cores, so count them by the wall length, not by the block count.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.

default.a: Count the courses and blocks per course, or divide the wall's face area by the face area of one block. Add buried base courses and about 5% to 10% for cuts and breakage.

default.q: How much gravel do I need behind a retaining wall?
default.a: Typically a 12 inch wide column of clean gravel behind the full wall height, plus a compacted gravel base under the first course. Taller or wetter sites may need more.

default.q: How tall can a DIY retaining wall be?
default.a: Model building codes commonly require a permit and engineered design above about 4 feet, measured from the footing to the top of the wall, and many towns set a lower limit of 2 to 3 feet. Walls that support a slope, driveway or building, and tiered walls, may need engineering even when they are shorter. Ask your local building department.

default.q: Do I need cap blocks?
default.a: Caps finish the top, hide the hollow cores and are glued in place. Count one per cap length along the wall.

default.q: Why does the first course matter so much?
default.a: Every block above depends on the first course being level and on a compacted base. A small error at the bottom becomes a visible lean at the top.

seo.title: Paver Base Calculator: Base Stone, Sand & Pavers
seo.description: Free paver base calculator. Enter patio size, base depth and paver dimensions to estimate base stone tons, bedding sand, number of pavers and total material cost.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate base stone, bedding sand, pavers and edge restraint for a patio or walkway.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A paver patio lasts when the base is right. Most paver failures, such as sinking, heaving and uneven joints, come from a thin or poorly compacted base rather than from the pavers themselves. A patio needs three things: a compacted layer of crushed stone, a thin layer of bedding sand, and the pavers with their joint sand.

This calculator estimates the base stone and bedding sand from your patio dimensions, including an allowance for compaction, and counts the pavers with an allowance for cuts. It also shows the materials cost and reminds you how much to excavate, because the base is the part you cannot easily fix later.

Edge restraint is the other detail that matters. Pavers need a restraint along every open edge to stop them spreading under foot traffic. The calculator shows the length needed, so you can plan it into the budget.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the patio length and width in feet.
Set the compacted base depth and the bedding sand depth in inches.
Enter the paver dimensions and an allowance for cuts and breakage.
Enter your prices to estimate the material cost.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Base cubic yards = area × base depth (ft) ÷ 27 × (1 + compaction)
Sand cubic yards = area × sand depth (ft) ÷ 27
Pavers = area ÷ one paver's area × (1 + waste)
Edge restraint = perimeter of the open edges
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Area. A 16 ft by 12 ft patio is 192 square feet.

Step 2: Base stone. A 6 inch compacted base is 192 × 0.5 = 96 cubic feet, or 3.6 cubic yards. A 20% compaction allowance brings it to about 4.3 cubic yards, or 6 tons at 1.4 tons per yard.

Step 3: Bedding sand. One inch of sand is 16 cubic feet, or 0.6 cubic yards, which is about 0.8 tons.

Step 4: Pavers. Each 9 by 6 inch paver covers 0.375 square feet, so 192 square feet needs 512 pavers. Adding 10% for cuts gives 564.

Step 5: Cost. At the default prices, base stone is about $239, sand about $36 and pavers about $705, a total of about $980. Excavate to the base depth plus the sand and the paver thickness, measured from the finished level.

fields.default:
Compact the base in lifts of no more than 2 to 4 inches, and check the surface with a level before you add sand.
Keep the bedding sand to about 1 inch. Do not use sand to fix a poor base.
Plan a slope of about 1/8 inch per foot away from buildings so rain runs off.
Use edge restraint along every open side so the pavers do not spread or creep outward over time.
Pavers are sold with a small allowance for breakage. Buy from the same batch so colours match.
