seo.title: Excavation Volume Calculator: Cubic Yards & Truck Loads
seo.description: Free excavation volume calculator. Enter length, width and depth to get cubic yards in place, loose volume after swell, weight in tons and number of truck loads.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Convert an excavation's length, width and depth to bank yards, loose yards, tons and truck loads.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Digging a hole removes a measurable volume of soil, but that soil takes up more space once it is loosened. Excavators work from in-place (bank) cubic yards, while trucks carry loose cubic yards, so both numbers matter when you plan hauling and quote disposal.

This calculator converts the size of the excavation into bank volume, applies a swell factor to find the loose volume, and estimates the weight and the number of truck loads. The result shows how many trips a job needs before you call a hauler.

The swell factor is the biggest source of error. Clay swells more than sand, and wet soil weighs more than dry. The calculator lets you enter your own values, so use a geotechnical report or local data if you have it.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length, width and depth of the excavation in feet.
Choose a swell factor for your soil type.
Enter the loose weight of the soil and the capacity of your trucks.
Read the bank volume, loose volume, number of loads and weight.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Bank cubic yards = length × width × depth ÷ 27
Loose cubic yards = bank yards × (1 + swell)
Weight (tons) = loose yards × loose weight per yard
Truck loads = loose yards ÷ truck capacity (rounded up)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Bank volume. A 40 ft by 30 ft excavation 4 ft deep is 4,800 cubic feet. Divided by 27, that is 177.8 bank cubic yards.

Step 2: Loose volume. With a 25% swell the soil fills 177.8 × 1.25, or about 222.2 loose cubic yards. That is the number a hauler needs to plan.

Step 3: Weight. At about 1.3 tons per loose yard, the spoil weighs about 289 tons.

Step 4: Truck loads. A 10 cubic yard truck carries 222.2 ÷ 10, which is 22.2, so you need 23 loads.

Step 5: Use. Those loads and weights are what you would send to a hauler or use to size a stockpile on site.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Swell is higher in clay and lower in sand and gravel. Use your geotechnical report or local data where you can.
Excavations with sloped sides contain more soil than vertical ones. Add the slope allowance to your dimensions.
Weight depends on moisture. Plan for the heaviest condition if you are working after rain.
Call 811 before you dig to locate buried utilities. Digging without that step is a legal and safety risk.
Plan for the spoil. Where it will go, and whether you can reuse it as fill, can change the cost more than the volume does.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do I calculate cubic yards of dirt?
default.a: Multiply length, width and depth in feet to get cubic feet, then divide by 27 to get cubic yards.

default.q: What is the swell factor in excavation?
default.a: It is the percentage by which soil expands when dug. Common soil swells about 25%, clay about 25% to 40% depending on moisture, and sand or gravel roughly 10% to 15%.

default.q: How many cubic yards does a dump truck hold?
default.a: A tandem truck commonly carries about 10 to 16 cubic yards of loose material, a single-axle about 5 to 8 and a tri-axle about 12 to 20, subject to weight limits.

default.q: How much does a cubic yard of dirt weigh?
default.a: Loose soil is often 1.1 to 1.5 tons per cubic yard, depending on moisture and type. Clay and wet soil are at the heavier end.

default.q: Why is the loose volume bigger than the hole?
default.a: Digging breaks the soil into pieces with air between them. Those gaps mean the same material takes up more space in a truck than it did in the ground.

seo.title: Dump Truck Load Calculator: How Many Loads Do You Need?
seo.description: Free dump truck load calculator. Enter material volume, weight and truck capacity to see how many loads you need and whether volume or weight is the limit.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Find how many truck loads you need, checking both bed volume and the weight limit.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A dump truck is limited by two things: the size of its bed and the weight it can legally carry. Light material such as mulch fills the bed before it reaches the weight limit. Heavy material such as wet clay or gravel can hit the weight limit with the bed only partly full, so a truck that looks big enough may still need extra trips.

This calculator checks both limits, tells you which one controls each load, and gives the number of loads and an estimated hauling cost. It is useful for planning the schedule and checking a hauler's quote before you agree to it.

The payload on paper is not always what a truck can carry on the road. Axle limits, bridge limits and local rules can reduce the legal load, so use the number your hauler gives you for your route.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the volume of material to move in loose cubic yards.
Enter the weight per cubic yard of the material.
Enter the truck's bed capacity and the payload limit.
Add the trucking cost per load to estimate hauling.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Weight of a full bed = bed volume × material weight per yard
Per-load yards = the smaller of the bed volume and payload ÷ material weight
Loads = total yards ÷ per-load yards (rounded up)
Hauling cost = loads × cost per load
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Total. You need to move 60 cubic yards of gravel at 1.4 tons per yard. That is 84 tons in total.

Step 2: Volume check. A 12 cubic yard bed filled with gravel would weigh 12 × 1.4 = 16.8 tons.

Step 3: Weight check. The truck's payload is 14 tons, so the bed cannot be filled. Weight is the limit, and each load carries 14 ÷ 1.4 = 10 cubic yards.

Step 4: Loads. 60 ÷ 10 = 6 loads. The truck carries 84 tons in six trips.

Step 5: Cost. At $175 a load, hauling costs about $1,050. Planning the trips this way shows the cost rises with weight, not bed size.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Ask your hauler for the real payload, which depends on the truck, its tyres and local limits.
Do not overload. Overloading is unsafe, damages roads and can result in fines.
Wet material weighs more. Plan for the heaviest condition, especially after rain.
Light material such as mulch or topsoil often fills the bed first, so volume is the limit for those loads.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How many cubic yards fit in a dump truck?
default.a: Roughly 5 to 8 for a single-axle truck, 10 to 16 for a tandem and 12 to 20 for a tri-axle, but heavy material may reach the weight limit first.

default.q: How many tons can a dump truck carry?
default.a: It varies by truck and state. Typical payloads are roughly 12 to 18 tons for tandems and 15 to 25 tons for tri-axles, limited by axle and bridge laws. Published figures vary, so confirm with the hauler.

default.q: Why does the calculator show weight as the limit?
default.a: Dense material such as gravel or wet soil can exceed the payload before the bed is full, so loads must be smaller than the bed volume.

default.q: Is it cheaper to haul in fewer, fuller loads?
default.a: Usually yes, but only within the legal limit. Overloading is not an option, so the cheapest plan is the one that uses the maximum legal load for the material.

default.q: How do I know how much a load weighs?
default.a: Use the density of your material. Ask the supplier for the weight per cubic yard, and check the truck's ticket after loading.

seo.title: Fill Dirt Calculator: Cubic Yards, Tons & Cost
seo.description: Free fill dirt calculator. Enter area and depth, allow for compaction, and get cubic yards to order, tons, truck loads and estimated cost including delivery.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate how much fill dirt to order, allowing for compaction, with tons, loads and cost.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Fill dirt settles and compacts after it is placed, so the amount you order has to be larger than the finished volume. Ordering exactly the finished volume usually leaves you short, and the shortfall is often discovered after the delivery fee has been paid.

This calculator works backward from the finished fill you need, applies a compaction allowance, and reports the cubic yards to order, the tons, the number of truck loads and the cost including delivery. It assumes the material is placed and compacted in layers.

Fill is not topsoil. Subsoil fill is good for raising or levelling ground, but a planting bed needs a layer of topsoil on top. The calculator covers the fill only, so add topsoil separately if you plan to plant.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length, width and finished depth of the area you need to fill, in feet and inches.
Set a compaction allowance, typically 10% to 20%.
Enter the loose weight of the dirt and your truck size.
Enter the price per yard and the delivery fee per load.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Finished yards = length × width × depth (in) ÷ 12 ÷ 27
Yards to order = finished yards ÷ (1 − compaction shrink)
Tons = yards to order × loose weight per yard
Cost = yards to order × price per yard + loads × delivery fee
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Finished volume. A 30 ft by 20 ft area raised by 12 inches is 600 cubic feet, or 22.2 cubic yards of finished fill.

Step 2: Order quantity. With 15% compaction shrink, you need to order 22.2 ÷ 0.85, about 26.1 cubic yards.

Step 3: Weight and loads. At 1.2 tons per yard, the order is about 31.4 tons. A 10 yard truck means 3 loads.

Step 4: Cost. At $18 a yard the material costs about $470. Delivery at $60 a load adds $180, so the total is about $651.

Step 5: Check. Compact in layers of 6 to 8 inches. If you compact the whole depth at once you will not reach the density you need.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Compact in thin layers, around 6 to 8 inches at a time, for the best result. Thick layers do not compact fully.
Use clean fill without debris, and ask the supplier what it contains. Old concrete or organic matter settles unevenly.
Fill dirt is not topsoil. Plan a layer of topsoil on top of the fill if you will plant.
Ask how the price is charged. Some suppliers quote by the load, some by the yard, and some by the ton.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much fill dirt do I need?
default.a: Multiply the area by the fill depth to get the finished volume, increase it by 10% to 20% for compaction, and convert to cubic yards.

default.q: How much does a cubic yard of fill dirt weigh?
default.a: Loose fill is typically about 1.1 to 1.4 tons per cubic yard, depending on moisture and soil type.

default.q: What is the difference between fill dirt and topsoil?
default.a: Fill dirt is subsoil used to raise or level ground and is not meant for planting. Topsoil is rich in organic matter and is placed on top for lawns and gardens.

default.q: Why is the compaction allowance so important?
default.a: Loose fill shrinks as it is compacted. Without an allowance, the finished area ends up lower than planned, and you need a second delivery.

default.q: Can I place fill in one thick layer?
default.a: It is better not to. Thick layers do not compact well at the bottom, and they settle unevenly later. Place and compact in thinner lifts.

seo.title: Excavation Cost Calculator: Digging, Hauling & Disposal
seo.description: Free excavation cost calculator. Estimate digging, hauling, disposal fees, machine delivery and contingency from the size of the excavation and your local rates.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Build a planning estimate for digging, hauling, dump fees and machine delivery.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Excavation prices vary widely with soil, access, distance to the dump and local labour costs, so a flat cost-per-yard figure can mislead. A better estimate breaks the job into digging, hauling, disposal and the delivery of the machine, then adds a contingency for surprises.

This calculator uses your own local rates, with editable defaults, to produce a planning estimate. It starts from the volume of the excavation, applies the swell factor and the truck capacity, and shows the total and the cost per in-place cubic yard so you can compare quotes.

The default prices are only examples. Use the calculator to see which line drives the cost. For many jobs, hauling and dump fees are larger than the digging itself, so reusing soil on site can save more than a cheaper machine.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the length, width and depth of the excavation, and the swell factor for the soil.
Enter the digging and loading rate per cubic yard.
Enter the truck capacity, the hauling cost per load and the dump fee per ton.
Add the machine delivery and a contingency, then read the total.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Digging = bank yards × digging rate
Hauling = loads × hauling rate per load
Disposal = loose yards × weight per yard × dump fee per ton
Total = (digging + hauling + disposal + delivery) × (1 + contingency)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Volume. A 40 ft by 30 ft excavation 4 ft deep is 177.8 bank yards, or about 222 loose yards after 25% swell. At 1.3 tons per yard that is about 289 tons, and 23 loads in a 10 yard truck.

Step 2: Digging. At $14 a bank yard, digging costs about $2,489.

Step 3: Hauling. At $175 a load, 23 loads cost about $4,025.

Step 4: Disposal and machine. A $12 a ton dump fee on 289 tons is about $3,467, and $350 for machine delivery brings the subtotal to about $10,331.

Step 5: Contingency. A 10% contingency adds about $1,033, for a total of about $11,364. That is about $64 per in-place cubic yard, but the figure changes sharply with haul distance and disposal costs.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
The default prices are illustrative. Replace them with quotes from local contractors and dump sites.
Keeping the soil on site, for example as fill, removes hauling and dump fees, which are often the largest costs.
Rock, groundwater and tight access can multiply digging costs. Use a larger contingency where those are likely.
Call 811 before you dig, and ask whether permits, shoring or a soil test are needed.
Compare quotes on the same basis: same volume, same disposal site and same contingency.
Estimates only. Material weights, prices and soil conditions vary by site and supplier. Call 811 before you dig, check local permits and building codes, and confirm quantities with your supplier or a qualified contractor.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much does excavation cost per cubic yard?
default.a: Digging alone is often priced in the low tens of dollars per cubic yard, but when hauling and disposal are included, the all-in cost per yard can be several times higher. It depends heavily on your area.

default.q: What affects excavation cost the most?
default.a: Hauling distance, disposal fees, soil type, depth, site access and whether rock or water is encountered. For many projects, hauling and disposal cost more than digging.

default.q: Can I reduce excavation costs?
default.a: Reusing soil on site, scheduling when machines are available and getting multiple quotes can all help. Ask whether the excavator can load directly into the trucks to save time.

default.q: Why should I include a contingency?
default.a: Unexpected rock, water, buried utilities and poor soil are common. A contingency of 10% to 20% covers many of these before they become a dispute with the contractor.

default.q: Is this a quote?
default.a: No. It is a planning estimate built from the rates you enter. Only a written quote from a licensed contractor shows the real price for your site.

seo.title: Compound Interest Calculator: Growth With Monthly Contributions
seo.description: Free compound interest calculator. Enter a starting balance, monthly contribution, rate and years to see your future balance, interest earned and value in today's money.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: See how a starting balance and regular contributions grow over time with compound interest.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Left alone, a balance grows faster each year because each year's gains are added to the base that earns the next year's gains. Over long periods this effect is larger than most people expect, which is why starting early and contributing regularly matters more than the exact starting amount.

This calculator models a starting balance plus monthly contributions at your chosen rate and compounding frequency. It shows the future balance, how much of it is your own money and how much is interest, and it adjusts for inflation so you can see the result in today's money rather than in future dollars.

The rate you enter is the most important assumption, and it is an estimate rather than a promise. Investment returns vary from year to year, and fees, taxes and inflation reduce what you keep. Test a few rates, including a cautious one, before relying on any single figure.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your starting balance and the amount you will add each month.
Enter the expected annual interest rate and how often interest compounds.
Set the number of years and an inflation estimate.
Read the future balance, the chart and the year-by-year table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Each month: balance = balance × (1 + monthly rate) + monthly contribution
Monthly rate = (1 + annual rate ÷ compounding periods per year)^(periods per year ÷ 12) − 1
Value in today's money = future balance ÷ (1 + inflation)^years
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Money you put in. A $10,000 starting balance plus $500 a month for 20 years is $10,000 + $500 × 240 months = $130,000 of your own money.

Step 2: Growth. At 6% a year compounded monthly, the balance grows to about $264,122 after 20 years.

Step 3: Interest. Subtract your $130,000 from the $264,122 and the interest earned is about $134,122. Interest is larger than the money you contributed.

Step 4: Early years. After two years the balance is about $23,988 on $22,000 contributed, so only about $1,988 of growth. The gap widens each year, which is why time matters so much.

Step 5: Real value. Adjusted for 2.5% yearly inflation, $264,122 is worth about $161,186 in today's money.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Time matters most. An extra five years of contributions often adds more than doubling the amount you save later.
Rates of return are not guaranteed. Test a lower rate to see a cautious case, and a higher one only as an optimistic check.
Fees reduce your effective return. Subtract them from the rate you enter, because a 1% annual fee can cut a long-term balance noticeably.
Taxes change the result. Tax-advantaged accounts and taxable accounts grow differently, so the rate should be after tax where it applies.
Compounding more often has a small effect. The rate and the time period matter far more than daily versus monthly compounding.
Results are estimates based on the numbers you enter and simplified assumptions. They are for education and planning and are not personal financial, tax or legal advice.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How is compound interest calculated?
default.a: Interest is added to the balance at each compounding period, and the next period's interest is calculated on the larger balance. With regular contributions, each deposit also starts earning interest from the day it is made.

default.q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
default.a: Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount. Compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus all interest earned so far, so it grows faster over time.

default.q: What is the rule of 72?
default.a: Dividing 72 by the annual rate gives a rough number of years to double your money. At 6%, it takes about 12 years.

default.q: Does compounding more often make a big difference?
default.a: Only slightly. Monthly versus yearly compounding at the same rate adds a small amount. The rate and the time period matter much more.

default.q: Why is the inflation-adjusted figure lower?
default.a: Inflation reduces what each future dollar can buy. The adjusted figure shows the balance in today's purchasing power, which is the more realistic measure for planning.

seo.title: Savings Goal Calculator: How Much to Save Each Month
seo.description: Free savings goal calculator. Enter your target, current savings, timeline and interest rate to find the monthly amount you need to save, with a chart and timeline comparison.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Find how much to save each month to reach a target amount by a set date.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A savings goal is easier to reach when it is turned into a monthly number. Whether you are saving for a down payment, a car or a trip, the amount to set aside depends on your target, the money you already have, how long you have and the interest your savings earn.

This calculator works backward from the goal. It tells you the monthly amount needed, accounting for your current savings and interest, and it shows how that amount changes with a shorter or longer timeline. That comparison is useful when the monthly figure is more than you can afford.

Interest helps less than people assume on a short goal. Over a few years the growth is a small share of the total, so most of the money has to come from your own deposits. Plan on that basis, then treat any interest as a bonus.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the amount you want to save and what you already have.
Choose how many years you have to reach the goal.
Enter the interest rate your savings earn.
Read the monthly amount, then compare the timelines in the table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Future value of current savings = current savings × (1 + monthly rate)^months
Monthly savings = (goal − future value of current savings) × monthly rate ÷ ((1 + monthly rate)^months − 1)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Gap. Your target is $50,000 in five years and you have $5,000 today. Growing at 4.5% a year, the $5,000 is worth about $6,250 by then, so the calculator needs to cover about $43,750 from new deposits and interest.

Step 2: Monthly amount. Spread over 60 months at 4.5%, the required deposit is about $651 a month.

Step 3: Money from you. Those deposits total about $39,086, which is the part of the goal you contribute directly.

Step 4: Interest. The rest of the growth, about $5,914 in total, comes from interest on your starting balance and deposits.

Step 5: Timeline comparison. The table shows about $3,655 a month over one year and $1,151 a month over three years, so a shorter goal needs a much larger monthly amount.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Automate the transfer on payday so saving happens before spending. Saving what is left at month end rarely works.
Match the account to the timeline. Short goals suit insured savings accounts, not volatile investments that could fall just before you need the money.
Rates change. Revisit the plan when your rate changes, because a lower rate means a higher monthly saving.
Build in a small buffer. Goals often cost more than expected, so aim slightly higher than the figure.
Results are estimates based on the numbers you enter and simplified assumptions. They are for education and planning and are not personal financial, tax or legal advice.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much should I save each month?
default.a: It depends on the goal, the timeline and your budget. Enter the target and time frame, and the calculator tells you the monthly amount needed.

default.q: Does interest really help with a short goal?
default.a: A little. Over one to three years, interest is a small share of the total, so most of the goal must come from your own deposits.

default.q: What if I cannot afford the monthly amount?
default.a: Try a longer timeline, a smaller goal, or a higher interest account, and see how the table changes. Even a few extra months can lower the monthly figure a lot.

default.q: Where should I keep savings for a goal?
default.a: Choose a safe, accessible account such as a high-yield savings account or a certificate of deposit that matches your date. Avoid investments that can fall sharply before you need the money.

default.q: Should I save for a goal or pay off debt first?
default.a: Debt with a high interest rate usually costs more than savings earn, so it often makes sense to reduce it first. Keep a small emergency cushion while you do.

seo.title: Debt Payoff Calculator: Snowball vs Avalanche
seo.description: Free debt payoff calculator. Enter up to three debts and an extra monthly payment to compare snowball and avalanche, see your debt-free date and the interest you save.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Compare the debt avalanche and debt snowball methods and see when you will be debt free.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
When you have several debts, the order in which you pay them changes how much interest you pay and how motivated you stay. The avalanche method puts any extra money toward the highest interest rate first. The snowball method targets the smallest balance first, which gives quick wins.

This calculator simulates both methods month by month, using each balance, interest rate and minimum payment. It shows the debt-free time and total interest for each method, and it also shows what would happen if you only paid the minimums, which is the baseline most people are on.

Whichever method you choose, the extra payment matters most. Money you send beyond the minimums cuts both the balance and the interest, and every debt you clear frees its minimum payment to roll into the next one.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the balance, interest rate and minimum payment for each debt. Use zero for unused rows.
Enter the extra amount you can pay each month above all minimums.
Compare the debt-free time and total interest for each strategy.
Pick the method you can stick with. The best plan is the one you finish.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Each month: interest = balance × annual rate ÷ 12
Pay each minimum, then send the extra money to the target debt
Avalanche target = highest interest rate. Snowball target = smallest balance.
When a debt is cleared, its minimum payment rolls into the next target
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: The debts. A $4,500 card at 22.9% with a $135 minimum, a $2,800 card at 18.5% with an $84 minimum and a $9,000 loan at 7.5% with a $180 minimum. Total debt is $16,300. Add a $150 extra payment for $549 a month in total.

Step 2: Monthly interest. In month one the card costs $4,500 × 22.9% ÷ 12 = $86, the second card $43 and the loan $56. That is about $185 of interest before any principal is repaid.

Step 3: Avalanche. Extra money goes to the 22.9% card first. Once it is gone, its payments roll into the 18.5% card, then the loan. The avalanche clears everything in about three years with about $3,060 of interest.

Step 4: Snowball. The snowball clears the $2,800 card first, then the $4,500 card, then the loan. It also takes three years but costs about $3,209, which is $149 more.

Step 5: Minimums only. Paying just the minimums takes 5 years and 1 month and costs about $5,705 in interest, so the $150 extra saves about $2,645 in interest with either method.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Avalanche saves the most interest. Snowball can give faster early wins, which helps some people stay motivated.
Keep making the minimum on every debt to avoid late fees and credit damage.
Stop adding new balances while you pay off the old ones, or the plan will not reduce your total debt.
Consider a lower-rate balance transfer or consolidation loan, but check the fees and the rate after any promotional period.
If your minimum does not cover the monthly interest, the balance grows. Increase the payment before it becomes unmanageable.
Results are estimates based on the numbers you enter and simplified assumptions. They are for education and planning and are not personal financial, tax or legal advice.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is the difference between the debt snowball and avalanche?
default.a: The snowball pays the smallest balance first for quick wins. The avalanche pays the highest-interest debt first and usually costs less in total interest.

default.q: Which method is better?
default.a: Avalanche is cheaper when rates differ a lot. Snowball may be better if you need early momentum. When balances and rates are similar, the difference is small.

default.q: What if my minimum payment does not cover interest?
default.a: Then the balance grows and the debt is never paid down. The calculator flags this, and you should increase the payment or talk to the lender about a plan.

default.q: Does this include new purchases?
default.a: No. It assumes you do not add new charges to the debts, so new spending would lengthen the payoff time.

default.q: Should I pay debt or invest?
default.a: Debt with a high interest rate, such as credit cards, usually costs more than typical investment returns, so paying it down first is often sensible. Low-rate debt may be better paired with investing.

seo.title: Salary to Hourly Calculator: Convert Annual Pay to Hourly Wage

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Convert an annual salary to an hourly rate and to monthly, biweekly, weekly and daily pay.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Comparing a salaried job with an hourly one starts with putting both on the same basis. Dividing a salary by the hours you actually work gives an hourly rate you can compare directly with a job advert or an offer.

This calculator turns an annual salary into an hourly rate using your hours per week and the weeks you are paid each year. It also shows the pay for each common period, daily, weekly, biweekly and monthly, before tax.

The result is only as good as the hours. A salary that looks high can work out to a modest hourly rate if you regularly work unpaid overtime, and an hourly wage can be worth more once paid holidays and benefits are counted. Use the calculator to see the baseline, then look at the full package. Commuting, professional memberships and work clothing reduce what the pay is worth, while paid leave and retirement matching add to it. For a salaried role, unpaid extra hours are the usual gap between the advertised salary and the real hourly rate, so count them honestly.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the annual salary before tax.
Enter the hours you work in a typical week.
Enter the weeks you are paid each year. Use 52 if holidays and vacation are paid.
Read the hourly rate and the pay for each period.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Hourly rate = annual salary ÷ (hours per week × weeks per year)
Weekly pay = annual salary ÷ weeks per year
Monthly pay = annual salary ÷ 12
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Paid hours. A standard full-time year is 40 hours a week for 52 weeks, which is 2,080 hours.

Step 2: Hourly rate. $65,000 ÷ 2,080 hours is $31.25 an hour.

Step 3: Daily and weekly. Over an eight-hour day that is $250 a day, and over a 40-hour week it is $1,250.

Step 4: Biweekly and monthly. Two weeks is $2,500, and dividing the annual salary by 12 gives $5,417 a month.

Step 5: Caveat. These are before tax. If you work 45 unpaid hours a week, the real rate falls to about $27.78 an hour.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.default:
Paid time off still counts toward the 2,080 hours, so use 52 weeks if you are paid for it.
If you regularly work unpaid overtime, use the real hours to see your true hourly rate.
Compare benefits as well as pay. Health insurance, retirement matching and paid leave add real value.

seo.title: Take-Home Pay Calculator: Estimate Your Paycheck After Taxes
seo.description: Free take-home pay calculator. Enter salary, tax rates and deductions to estimate your net pay per paycheck, per month and per year, with a breakdown of where the money goes.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate your paycheck after taxes, retirement contributions and benefits.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Your salary is not what lands in your bank account. Income taxes, Social Security and Medicare, retirement contributions and health premiums all come out first. Some of those deductions reduce your taxable income, which changes how much tax you pay as well.

This calculator estimates net pay from the effective tax rates you enter. Because tax rules change and vary by state, it does not apply official tax tables. It lets you set the rates yourself, so you can use numbers from your last tax return or your pay stub.

Two numbers matter most: your effective federal and state tax rates, and whether each deduction is taken before or after tax. Getting those right will bring the estimate close to your real paycheck. Your state may have no income tax, a flat rate or a local tax on top, and each of those changes the answer, so enter the rate that actually applies to you.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your gross salary and how many pay periods you have each year.
Enter your effective federal and state tax rates. You can find them on your last tax return.
Enter Social Security and Medicare, which is usually 7.65% of wages.
Add retirement contributions, health premiums and other deductions, and say whether each is pre-tax.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Taxable income = gross pay − pre-tax retirement − pre-tax health insurance
Income tax = taxable income × (federal rate + state rate)
Social Security and Medicare = (gross pay − pre-tax health insurance) × FICA rate
Take-home = gross pay − taxes − all deductions
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Gross. A $75,000 salary paid 26 times a year.

Step 2: Pre-tax deductions. Retirement at 5% is $3,750, and $150 a month for health insurance is $1,800 a year. Taxable income is $75,000 − $3,750 − $1,800 = $69,450.

Step 3: Income taxes. Federal at 13% of $69,450 is about $9,029, and state at 4% is $2,778.

Step 4: Payroll taxes. At 7.65% of $73,200 (salary less health premiums), FICA is about $5,600.

Step 5: Net pay. $75,000 − $9,029 − $2,778 − $5,600 − $3,750 − $1,800 = $52,044 a year, or $4,337 a month and $2,002 per paycheck. That is about 69% of gross pay.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use your effective tax rate (total tax divided by taxable income), not your top bracket, because the lower brackets apply to the first part of your income.
Your pay stub shows exact amounts. Use it to refine the rates and check the deductions.
Pre-tax contributions lower your taxable income, so they cost less take-home pay than their face value.
Social Security tax stops above an annual wage limit, so very high earners will pay less than 7.65% on the top portion.
Results are estimates based on the numbers you enter and simplified assumptions. They are for education and planning and are not personal financial, tax or legal advice.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do I calculate take-home pay?
default.a: Subtract pre-tax deductions from gross pay, apply income taxes to what remains, subtract payroll taxes, then subtract any after-tax deductions.

default.q: What is an effective tax rate?
default.a: It is your total income tax divided by your taxable income. It is lower than your top bracket rate because the first dollars are taxed at lower rates.

default.q: Why is my paycheck smaller than expected?
default.a: Common reasons are higher retirement contributions, benefit premiums, or withholding that differs from your actual tax rate.

default.q: Does this calculator use official tax tables?
default.a: No. You enter your own effective rates. For exact withholding, use your employer's payroll tools or an official tax calculator.

default.q: Why does pre-tax versus after-tax matter?
default.a: A pre-tax deduction lowers the income that is taxed, so it reduces take-home pay by less than the deduction itself. An after-tax deduction reduces take-home pay by the full amount.

seo.title: 50/30/20 Budget Calculator: Needs, Wants & Savings
seo.description: Free 50/30/20 budget calculator. Enter your monthly take-home pay and spending to see how it compares with the 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings rule.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Split your income into needs, wants and savings and see how your spending compares.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
The 50/30/20 rule is a simple way to plan a budget: about 50% of your after-tax income for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and extra debt payments. It is a starting point rather than a law, and many households adjust the split to fit their costs.

This calculator gives you the target amount for each category based on your take-home pay, and compares those targets with what you actually spend. It shows the gap in each category, so you can see where to adjust first.

The rule works best with real numbers. Track a month of spending before you set targets, because most people underestimate their wants and overestimate what they save. Start by listing fixed bills, then variable essentials such as groceries and fuel, and only then discretionary spending. Irregular costs, such as car repairs, annual insurance premiums and holiday gifts, are easy to forget, so divide them by twelve and budget a monthly amount for each. A budget that includes them is far more likely to survive a busy month.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your monthly take-home income after taxes.
Enter what you spend on needs, wants, and savings or extra debt payments.
Compare each category with its 50%, 30% and 20% target.
Adjust the categories that are furthest from their targets.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Needs target = take-home income × 50%
Wants target = take-home income × 30%
Savings and debt target = take-home income × 20%
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Targets. On $4,500 a month, the targets are $2,250 for needs, $1,350 for wants and $900 for savings and debt.

Step 2: Actual spending. Suppose you spend $2,600 on needs, $1,300 on wants and $600 on savings.

Step 3: Comparison. Needs are $350 over target, wants are $50 under and savings are $300 under.

Step 4: Priority. The savings gap is the biggest. Moving $300 from wants and needs into savings would bring the split close to the rule.

Step 5: Percentages. Needs are 58% of income, wants 29% and savings 13%, so the budget is over on needs and short on savings.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
In high-cost areas, needs can exceed 50%. Adjust the split to fit, for example 60/20/20, and keep the savings share as high as you can.
Count minimum debt payments as needs and extra debt payments as savings, so the categories reflect where the money goes.
Track your real spending for a month to fill the numbers with facts rather than estimates.
Review the split every few months. Income changes and so do fixed costs such as rent and insurance.

seo.title: Emergency Fund Calculator: How Much Do You Need?
seo.description: Free emergency fund calculator. Enter essential monthly expenses, months of cover and your savings to see your target, the shortfall and how long it will take to reach.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out how big your emergency fund should be and how long it will take to build.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
An emergency fund is money set aside for job loss, medical bills or urgent repairs, so you do not have to borrow at high interest when something goes wrong. How much you need depends on your essential expenses and how stable your income is.

This calculator sets a target from your essential monthly expenses and the number of months you want covered. It shows how many months your current savings would cover, the shortfall, and how long it will take to close the gap with regular saving and interest.

Only essential spending belongs in the calculation. Rent, food, utilities, transport, insurance and minimum debt payments are essential, while dining out and subscriptions are not, because you can cut them in a crisis. A simple test is to ask whether a bill would still be due if you lost your income next month. If yes, it belongs in the total. A crisis often brings extra costs too, such as travel, childcare or replacing a broken appliance, so a little headroom above the plain expense total is sensible.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your essential monthly expenses.
Choose how many months of expenses you want covered.
Enter your current savings, your monthly contribution and the interest rate your savings earn.
Read the target, the shortfall and the time needed to reach it.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Target = essential monthly expenses × months of cover
Months covered today = current savings ÷ essential monthly expenses
Each month: balance = balance × (1 + monthly rate) + monthly contribution
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Target. Essential expenses of $3,200 a month and a six-month goal give a target of $19,200.

Step 2: Today. $2,500 of savings covers about 0.8 months, so the shortfall is $16,700.

Step 3: Saving. Adding $400 a month at 4% interest, the balance reaches $19,200 in about 3 years and 3 months.

Step 4: Smaller goals. The table shows that three months of cover needs $9,600, leaving a shortfall of $7,100 today.

Step 5: Choice. If your income is steady, six months may be enough. If it is irregular, aim higher, which means a longer build time.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Count only essentials, not every expense. You can cut the rest in an emergency, and that keeps the target realistic.
Keep the fund in an easily accessible insured account, not in volatile investments that could fall when you need the money.
Self-employed or single-income households may want more than six months, because a gap in income lasts longer.
Build a small starter fund first, then grow it. Even one month of cover is a useful buffer against a common shock.
Results are estimates based on the numbers you enter and simplified assumptions. They are for education and planning and are not personal financial, tax or legal advice.

default.q: Where should I keep an emergency fund?
default.a: In a safe, liquid account such as a high-yield savings account, where you can withdraw quickly without market risk.

default.a: Many people build a small starter fund first, then pay down high-interest debt, then grow the fund. The right order depends on your situation and the interest rate on the debt.

fields.label: Tagline

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A car payment depends on more than the sticker price. Sales tax, dealer fees, your down payment and trade-in, the interest rate and the length of the loan all change what you pay each month and in total. Many buyers focus on the monthly figure and miss how much the loan adds to the cost of the car.

This calculator builds the amount financed from the price, the trade-in, tax and fees, subtracts your down payment, and shows your monthly payment, total interest and the full cost of the vehicle. A table compares the same loan over terms from 36 to 84 months, which shows the trade-off between a lower payment and more interest.

Get a rate from your bank or credit union before you visit a dealer. A pre-approved rate gives you a benchmark, so you can check any dealer financing offer against a number you already have.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the vehicle price, your down payment and any trade-in value.
Enter the loan rate (APR) and the term in months.
Enter sales tax and any title, registration or dealer fees.
Compare the payment and interest for different terms in the table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Amount financed = price − trade-in + sales tax + fees − down payment
Monthly payment = loan × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months
Total interest = monthly payment × months − amount financed
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Amount financed. A $32,000 car with $4,000 down and a $3,000 trade-in. Sales tax at 6.5% on the $29,000 after trade-in is about $1,885, and $600 of fees adds to the total. $32,000 − $3,000 + $1,885 + $600 − $4,000 = $27,485 to finance.

Step 2: Payment. At 7% over 60 months the payment is about $544 a month.

Step 3: Interest. Total payments over 60 months are about $32,654, which is $5,169 more than the amount financed.

Step 4: Total cost. The car costs about $39,654 including your $7,000 of down payment and trade-in.

Step 5: Longer term. At 84 months the payment falls to about $415 a month, but interest rises to about $7,360. At 36 months the payment is about $849 and interest about $3,067.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
A longer term lowers the payment but increases interest, and it can leave you owing more than the car is worth for longer.
Look at the total cost, not just the monthly payment. Dealers can often hit a monthly target by stretching the term.
Negotiate the price of the car before discussing financing, so the two are not mixed together.
Gap insurance can matter on a long loan with a small down payment, because the car can lose value faster than you repay the loan.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
A lease payment covers the part of the car's value you use up, plus a finance charge and tax. The terms dealers quote, money factor and residual value, are less familiar than an interest rate, which makes leases hard to compare with each other and with a loan.

This calculator turns those terms into a monthly payment. It shows the depreciation and finance charge separately, converts the money factor into an approximate APR, and totals the cost of the lease, including the amount due at signing.

Leasing is a rental of the car's use, not a purchase. At the end you return the car, or pay the residual to buy it. Work out the total cost of the lease and compare it with the cost of owning the same car for the same period.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the MSRP and the negotiated price of the car.
Enter your down payment and any acquisition fees.
Enter the residual value as a percentage of MSRP, the money factor and the lease term.
Enter the sales tax rate that applies to lease payments in your state.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Capitalized cost = negotiated price + fees − down payment
Depreciation per month = (capitalized cost − residual value) ÷ months
Finance charge per month = (capitalized cost + residual value) × money factor
Payment = (depreciation + finance charge) × (1 + tax rate)
Approximate APR = money factor × 2,400
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Capitalized cost. The car is negotiated to $35,000, plus $695 of fees, less $2,000 down. That gives $33,695.

Step 2: Residual. A 60% residual on the $36,000 MSRP is $21,600, the value the lessor expects at the end.

Step 3: Depreciation. ($33,695 − $21,600) ÷ 36 months is about $336 a month.

Step 4: Finance charge. ($33,695 + $21,600) × 0.0025 is about $138 a month. The money factor of 0.0025 is roughly a 6% APR.

Step 5: Payment and total. ($336 + $138) × 1.065 is about $505 a month. Over 36 months that is about $18,180, plus the $2,000 down, a total lease cost of about $20,181.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Negotiate the price of the car, not just the monthly payment. A lower capitalized cost lowers the payment.
Ask for the money factor and residual value in writing and convert the factor to APR to compare with loans.
Check the mileage allowance and the charges for excess miles and wear, which can be large at the end.
A higher residual value lowers the depreciation you pay, but check whether the lessor has set it high on purpose to make the payment look low.

seo.title: Fuel Cost Calculator: Cost Per Mile, Month & Trip
seo.description: Free fuel cost calculator. Enter miles, fuel economy and fuel price to get your cost per mile, monthly and yearly fuel spend, and the cost of a trip.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out the cost per mile, per month and per trip from your fuel economy and fuel price.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Fuel is one of the biggest running costs of a car, and it moves with both fuel prices and how much you drive. Knowing your cost per mile helps you budget for commuting and road trips, and it makes it easier to compare the running costs of different vehicles.

This calculator turns your monthly miles, fuel economy and fuel price into a cost per mile, a monthly and yearly total, and the fuel cost of a specific trip. A table shows how your monthly spend changes if fuel prices move up or down.

The sticker fuel economy is a best case. Real driving, with stop-start traffic, cold weather, roof racks and a heavy foot, often gives a lower mpg, so the figure you enter should reflect how you actually drive. To find your real figure, fill the tank, note the odometer, and fill it again at the same level after your next full tank. Divide the miles by the gallons added, and average two or three tanks. Motorway trips and short city journeys often give different figures, so calculate both if your driving is mixed.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the miles you drive in a typical month.
Enter your fuel economy in miles per gallon.
Enter the price per gallon.
Enter a trip distance to see the fuel cost of that journey.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Cost per mile = fuel price ÷ miles per gallon
Monthly cost = miles per month ÷ miles per gallon × fuel price
Trip cost = trip miles ÷ miles per gallon × fuel price
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Cost per mile. At 28 mpg and $3.60 a gallon, each mile costs $3.60 ÷ 28, about $0.129.

Step 2: Monthly. Driving 1,000 miles a month costs about $129, which is $1,543 a year.

Step 3: Gallons. A 300-mile trip uses 300 ÷ 28, about 10.7 gallons.

Step 4: Trip cost. 10.7 gallons at $3.60 is about $39 for the trip.

Step 5: Price sensitivity. The table shows that at $3.00 a gallon the monthly cost is about $107, and at $3.50 about $125, so a 50-cent change in price adds about $18 a month here.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Real mpg is often lower than the sticker figure in city driving, in cold weather and at high speeds. Track a few tanks to find your own figure.
Keep tyres properly inflated and remove unneeded weight. Both improve fuel economy at little cost.
Use the price table to see how a rise in fuel prices would affect your budget.
Combining short trips and avoiding long idling reduces the fuel you burn without changing how far you drive.
Results are estimates from the numbers you enter. Dealer quotes, lender terms, taxes and fees vary, so confirm with the dealer or lender before you sign.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do I calculate fuel cost per mile?
default.a: Divide the price of a gallon of fuel by your car's miles per gallon. At $3.60 and 28 mpg that is about 12.9 cents per mile.

default.q: How much does it cost to drive 100 miles?
default.a: Multiply the cost per mile by 100. At 12.9 cents a mile, 100 miles costs about $12.86 in fuel.

default.q: How can I lower my fuel costs?
default.a: Drive smoothly, maintain your car, reduce idling, combine trips and choose a more efficient vehicle when you replace it.

default.q: Does fuel economy change in winter?
default.a: Yes. Cold weather reduces efficiency, especially on short trips when the engine stays cold, so winter fuel costs are often higher than the summer figure.

default.q: Should I use the sticker mpg?
default.a: It is a useful starting point, but real mpg is usually lower. Calculate from your own fuel records for the most accurate budget.

seo.title: EV Charging Cost Calculator: Electric vs Gas Fuel Cost
seo.description: Free EV charging cost calculator. Enter miles, efficiency, home and public charging prices to see your yearly charging cost and savings compared with a gas car.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate yearly electric vehicle charging costs and compare them with a gas car.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Charging an electric car usually costs far less than fuelling a gas car, but the savings depend on your electricity rate and on how much you rely on public fast chargers, which are often priced at two to three times the home rate.

This calculator estimates the energy your EV uses, including charging losses, splits it between home and public charging, and compares the yearly cost with a gas car at the fuel price you enter. It shows the yearly savings and the cost per mile.

Charging losses are easy to overlook. Some energy is lost as heat between the outlet and the battery, so you pay for more electricity than the car uses to drive. The calculator adds that loss to the energy used.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the miles you drive each year and your EV's efficiency in miles per kWh.
Enter the share of charging you do at home and the home and public prices per kWh.
Enter the gas car's fuel economy and the gas price to compare.
Read the yearly cost, the savings and the cost per mile.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Energy used = miles ÷ miles per kWh × (1 + charging losses)
EV cost = home kWh × home price + public kWh × public price
Gas cost = miles ÷ mpg × gas price
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Energy. 12,000 miles at 3.5 miles per kWh is about 3,429 kWh. Adding 10% charging losses gives about 3,771 kWh a year.

Step 2: Split. 80% at home is about 3,017 kWh at $0.17, costing about $513. 20% at public chargers is about 754 kWh at $0.45, costing about $339.

Step 3: EV total. $513 + $339 is about $852 a year.

Step 4: Gas comparison. A 30 mpg car covers 12,000 miles on 400 gallons, which at $3.60 costs about $1,440.

Step 5: Savings. The EV saves about $588 a year in fuel, or about $49 a month. If you charged only at public stations, the savings would be much smaller.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Home charging overnight on a time-of-use plan can be much cheaper than the average rate, so check your utility's tariffs.
Public fast charging often costs two to three times as much per kWh as home charging, so the more you use it, the less you save.
Cold weather and high speeds reduce range and efficiency, so the real miles per kWh can be lower than the rated figure.
Fuel is only part of the cost. Compare purchase price, insurance and maintenance too, because the total picture is what matters.
Results are estimates from the numbers you enter. Dealer quotes, lender terms, taxes and fees vary, so confirm with the dealer or lender before you sign.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.a: It depends on your electricity rate and the car's efficiency. At $0.17 per kWh and 3.5 miles per kWh, home charging costs about 5 cents per mile.

seo.title: Car Depreciation Calculator: Estimated Value by Year
seo.description: Free car depreciation calculator. Enter the price and yearly depreciation rates to see the estimated value, total loss and monthly cost of depreciation over time.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Estimate how much value a car loses each year and what it may be worth when you sell.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Depreciation is usually the largest cost of owning a new car, and it happens quietly. A car loses the most value in its first year and keeps losing value each year after, though more slowly. The loss is a real cost even though you never write a cheque for it.

This calculator applies a first-year rate and a yearly rate for later years to estimate the car's value over the time you own it. It reports the total loss and expresses the loss as a monthly cost, which you can compare with the monthly cost of a loan or lease.

Depreciation varies widely between models. Some hold their value well and others lose it quickly, so the rates you enter should come from recent sales data for the specific model, not from a general rule.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the purchase price.
Enter the first-year depreciation rate and the yearly rate for later years.
Enter how many years you plan to own the car.
Read the estimated value, the total loss and the year-by-year table.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Value after year 1 = price × (1 − first-year rate)
Value after each later year = previous value × (1 − yearly rate)
Total depreciation = price − value at the end of ownership
Monthly cost = total depreciation ÷ months owned
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Year one. A $35,000 car losing 20% in the first year is worth $28,000 after one year, a loss of $7,000.

Step 2: Years two and three. At 12% a year, it is worth $24,640 after two years and about $21,683 after three.

Step 3: Years four and five. It is about $19,081 after four years and $16,791 after five.

Step 4: Total loss. Over five years the car loses about $18,209, which is 52% of the price.

Step 5: Monthly cost. Spread over 60 months, the depreciation is about $303 a month, a cost that applies whether or not you sell.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Real depreciation depends on the make, model, mileage, condition and market. Check recent listings for the model you want.
Buying a used car lets the first owner absorb the steepest drop, which is one reason used cars can be good value.
Include depreciation when you compare buying and leasing, because a lease payment is largely depreciation.
Keep records of maintenance. A documented service history helps a car hold its value when you sell.
Results are estimates from the numbers you enter. Dealer quotes, lender terms, taxes and fees vary, so confirm with the dealer or lender before you sign.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How much does a car depreciate in the first year?
default.a: New cars commonly lose around 15% to 25% in the first year, then a smaller share each year after, though it varies widely by model.

default.q: Do all cars depreciate at the same rate?
default.a: No. Some trucks and certain models hold value well, while luxury cars and some EVs may lose value faster.

default.q: How can I reduce the effect of depreciation?
default.a: Buy a car that is one to three years old, choose a model with a strong resale record, and keep it well maintained with sensible mileage.

default.q: Does depreciation matter if I keep the car a long time?
default.a: The first few years carry most of the loss, so keeping a car for many years spreads that cost across more miles and lowers the cost per year.

default.q: Is the estimate the same as the resale price?
default.a: No. Dealers and private buyers pay different amounts, and condition, mileage and local demand all affect the final price.

seo.title: Markup and Margin Calculator: Profit Margin & Pricing
seo.description: Free markup and margin calculator. Enter cost and selling price to get gross margin, markup and profit, plus the price you need for any target margin.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Convert between cost, price, markup and gross margin, and find the price for a target margin.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Markup and margin both describe profit, but they use different bases, and mixing them up is a common and costly pricing mistake. Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price. The same sale can show a 50% markup and only a 33% margin.

This calculator shows both for the cost and price you enter, works out the gross profit at your expected sales volume, and lists the selling price you need to reach a target margin. Use it before you set prices, not after, because a small change in price can change the margin a great deal.

Gross margin is only the first layer of profit. It does not include rent, wages, shipping you pay, marketing or card fees, so a healthy gross margin can still produce a loss once overheads are counted. Prices should also leave room for returns, damaged stock and promotions. A product that sells well at a 40% margin can still lose money if a tenth of units are returned for a full refund, so build a small allowance into the cost.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the cost to you of each unit.
Enter the price you sell it for.
Enter the number of units you expect to sell.
Use the table to see the price needed for different target margins.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Profit = selling price − cost
Margin = profit ÷ selling price
Markup = profit ÷ cost
Price for a target margin = cost ÷ (1 − target margin)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Profit per unit. An item costing $60 and selling for $100 earns $40.

Step 2: Margin. $40 ÷ $100 is a 40% margin, the share of each sale kept as gross profit.

Step 3: Markup. $40 ÷ $60 is a 66.7% markup, the profit measured against cost.

Step 4: Volume. Selling 200 units at $40 profit each gives $8,000 of gross profit before overheads.

Step 5: Target price. For a 50% margin on a $60 cost, the price must be $60 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = $120.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
A 50% markup is not a 50% margin. A 50% markup gives a 33.3% margin, so check which one a supplier or customer is quoting.
Gross margin ignores overhead. Make sure it covers rent, salaries, shipping, marketing and card fees.
Review prices regularly as costs change, and do not let a supplier price rise pass through unnoticed.
Discounts reduce margin faster than most people expect. A 20% discount on a 40% margin leaves only a 25% margin.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: What is the difference between markup and margin?
default.a: Markup is profit divided by cost. Margin is profit divided by selling price. For the same sale, the markup percentage is always higher than the margin percentage.

default.q: How do I calculate a selling price from a margin?
default.a: Divide your cost by one minus the margin. For a $60 cost and a 40% margin, the price is $60 ÷ 0.60 = $100.

default.q: What is a good profit margin?
default.a: It varies by industry. Retail often works with gross margins of 20% to 50%, while software can be far higher. Compare with your sector and your overheads.

default.q: How does a discount affect margin?
default.a: A discount comes straight out of the price, so it removes profit dollar for dollar. Work out the margin at the discounted price before offering it.

default.q: Should I price by markup or by margin?
default.a: Margin is better for judging profitability against revenue, while markup is common when you apply a set percentage to cost. Use margin when you want a clear target for the business.

seo.title: Break-Even Calculator: Break-Even Units & Revenue
seo.description: Free break-even calculator. Enter fixed costs, price and variable cost per unit to find break-even units and sales, and the volume needed for a target profit.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Find how many units you must sell to cover costs, and how many to reach a profit target.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
The break-even point is the sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs. Below it you lose money, above it you make a profit. It is one of the first numbers to know before launching or pricing a product, because it shows how much you must sell just to stand still.

This calculator divides your fixed costs by the contribution each unit makes after its variable costs. It shows the units and sales needed to break even, the volume needed for a profit target, and a chart of profit at different volumes.

Fixed and variable costs are where most mistakes happen. Fixed costs include the things you pay whether or not you sell, such as rent, insurance, software and loan repayments. Variable costs rise with each sale, such as materials, packaging and shipping.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter your fixed costs for the period, for example per month.
Enter the selling price and the variable cost of each unit.
Enter the profit you want to earn in the same period.
Read the break-even volume and study the chart.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit
Break-even sales = break-even units × selling price
Units for a profit target = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Contribution. A $45 price and $18 of variable cost leaves $27 per unit toward fixed costs.

Step 2: Break-even units. $12,000 of monthly fixed costs ÷ $27 is about 444 units, which rounds up to 445.

Step 3: Break-even sales. 445 units at $45 is about $20,000 of revenue a month.

Step 4: Profit target. To earn $3,000 a month on top of covering costs, you need ($12,000 + $3,000) ÷ $27, which is about 556 units.

Step 5: Use. Each extra unit above 445 adds $27 of profit, so the table and chart show how quickly profit grows once you pass the break-even point.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Include every fixed cost, such as rent, wages, insurance, software and loan payments, or the break-even point will be too low.
Raising the price or cutting the variable cost lowers the break-even point quickly, often more than a small increase in sales would.
Check that the break-even volume is realistic for your market. A break-even point larger than your likely sales means the plan needs changing.
Revisit the numbers when costs change, especially when a supplier raises prices.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do you calculate the break-even point?
default.a: Divide fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit, which is the price minus the variable cost per unit.

default.q: What are fixed and variable costs?
default.a: Fixed costs stay the same regardless of sales, such as rent. Variable costs rise with each unit sold, such as materials and shipping.

default.q: What if the break-even point is too high?
default.a: Raise the price, reduce fixed or variable costs, or find ways to increase volume. Test each change in the calculator to see which one matters most.

default.q: Is break-even revenue the same as break-even units?
default.a: They describe the same point in different ways. Units tell you how many to sell, and revenue tells you how much money that means at your price.

default.q: Does break-even include taxes?
default.a: No. It is a pre-tax figure. Income tax on profit means you need to earn more than break-even to keep a given amount after tax.

seo.title: Sales Tax Calculator: Add or Remove Tax From a Price
seo.description: Free sales tax calculator. Enter a price and tax rate to see the sales tax and total, or find the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive amount, with a table of rates.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Add sales tax to a price, or work out the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive total.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Sales tax is added at the register in most US states, but rates differ by state, county and city, and some items are exempt or taxed differently. Knowing how to add tax to a price, and how to take it back out of a total, is useful for shoppers and small businesses alike.

This calculator adds tax to a pre-tax price and quantity and shows the total. It also works out the pre-tax price when the number you have already includes tax, and it shows how the total changes at different rates.

The rate that applies is your combined rate for the exact address where the sale happens, which can be different from the rate in the next town. Check it before you rely on the figure for pricing or for filing. In most states the tax is calculated on the price after any discount applied before the sale, not on the list price, while a rebate paid later usually does not reduce the tax. If a store shows prices with tax included, divide by one plus the rate to see the pre-tax figure, which is the number to compare with a supplier quote.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the price before tax and the quantity.
Enter the combined sales tax rate for your location.
Read the tax and the total, and the pre-tax price if the entered price already includes tax.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Sales tax = price × quantity × tax rate
Total = price × quantity + sales tax
Pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive price = tax-inclusive price ÷ (1 + tax rate)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Tax. A $249.99 item at an 8.25% sales tax rate has tax of $249.99 × 0.0825, which is about $20.62.

Step 2: Total. $249.99 + $20.62 = $270.61 at the register.

Step 3: Reverse. If $249.99 already included tax, the pre-tax price is $249.99 ÷ 1.0825, or about $230.94.

Step 4: Check. Adding 8.25% to $230.94 gives back about $249.99, which confirms the reverse calculation.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Use the combined state and local rate for your exact location, not only the state rate.
Check whether your goods or services are taxable. Rules vary by product and by jurisdiction, and some services are taxed in some states and not in others.
Businesses that sell across state lines may have registration and filing obligations. Ask an accountant before you start.
Round tax the way your point-of-sale system does, so your receipts and your records agree.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.
fields.help: One tip per line.

default.q: How do you calculate sales tax?
default.a: Multiply the price by the tax rate as a decimal. For 8.25%, multiply by 0.0825. Add that to the price for the total.

default.q: How do I remove sales tax from a total?
default.a: Divide the total by one plus the tax rate. For a total of $270.61 at 8.25%, divide by 1.0825 to get about $250.

default.q: Is sales tax the same everywhere?
default.a: No. Rates differ by state, county and city, and some states have no state sales tax. Check your local combined rate.

default.q: Does the tax apply to the quantity or to each item?
default.a: The tax applies to the total taxable amount, so for multiple items the tax is the price times the quantity times the rate.

default.q: Why is my final price different from this calculator?
default.a: Local rates change, some items are exempt, and some stores round each line item differently. Compare against your receipt for the exact figure.

seo.title: Freelance Hourly Rate Calculator: What Should You Charge?
seo.description: Free freelance hourly rate calculator. Enter your income goal, expenses, tax set-aside, billable hours and time off to find the hourly rate you need to charge.

fields.label: Tagline
fields.default: Work out the hourly rate you need to charge to reach your income goal after expenses and tax.

fields.label: Intro
fields.default:
Freelancers often set rates by looking at an employee's hourly pay, but that leaves out business expenses, taxes, unpaid time off and the hours spent finding clients and doing admin. As a result, many freelancers undercharge and then struggle to make the numbers work.

This calculator works backward from the income you want to take home. It adds taxes and expenses to find the revenue you need, then divides that by your real billable hours to give an hourly rate. It also shows how much you need to bill each week.

Billable hours are the most sensitive input. A freelancer who can bill 15 hours a week needs a much higher rate than one who can bill 25, so be realistic about how much of the working week is paid client work.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Steps
fields.default:
Enter the yearly take-home income you want.
Enter your yearly business expenses and the share of profit you set aside for tax and retirement.
Enter the billable hours you work per week and the weeks you take off each year.
Read the hourly rate and the revenue target, and compare different billable hours.
fields.help: One step per line.

fields.label: Formulas
fields.default:
Profit needed = take-home income ÷ (1 − tax set-aside)
Revenue needed = profit needed + business expenses
Hourly rate = revenue needed ÷ (billable hours per week × weeks worked)
fields.help: One formula per line.

fields.label: Worked example
fields.default:
Step 1: Profit. To take home $70,000 with 25% set aside for tax and retirement, you need $70,000 ÷ 0.75, about $93,333 of profit.

Step 2: Revenue. Add $8,000 of business expenses to reach about $101,333 of revenue.

Step 3: Billable hours. Billing 25 hours a week for 46 working weeks is 1,150 hours.

Step 4: Rate. $101,333 ÷ 1,150 is about $88.12 an hour, or about $2,203 a week of revenue.

Step 5: Sensitivity. If you could bill only 15 hours a week, the rate would need to be about $146.86 an hour to reach the same income.
fields.help: Separate paragraphs with a blank line.

fields.label: Tips
fields.default:
Count only billable hours. Sales, admin and learning rarely fit inside client time, so a 25-hour billable week is already a full week.
Include unpaid holidays, sick days and slow periods in your weeks off, so the annual figure is realistic.
Consider project or value-based pricing once you know your minimum hourly rate, since clients often pay for results rather than hours.
Set aside money for tax as you earn it. Self-employed income is usually taxed without an employer withholding it.
Results are estimates for planning and education. They are not accounting, tax or legal advice. Check rates and rules with your accountant or local tax authority.

default.q: How much should a freelancer charge per hour?
default.a: Enough to cover your income goal, business expenses, taxes and unpaid time. This calculator shows the rate that does that for your numbers.

default.q: Why is a freelance rate higher than an employee's hourly rate?
default.a: Freelancers pay their own taxes and insurance, cover their own expenses, have no paid time off and cannot bill every working hour.

default.q: How many hours can a freelancer bill in a week?
default.a: Many freelancers bill 20 to 30 hours in a full working week. The rest goes to admin, marketing and finding work.

default.q: Should I quote by the hour or by the project?
default.a: Hourly rates are simple and protect you on uncertain work, while fixed project prices reward efficiency. Use the hourly rate as a floor when you price projects.

default.q: How often should I raise my rates?
default.a: Review rates at least once a year, and whenever your costs or the demand for your work change.
